88215.q: What did two crystal hunters find on the Planggenstock in the canton of Uri in 2005?
a: A huge treasure of rock crystals
A gold mine from Roman times
88215.e: In 2005, Franz von Arx and Paul von Känel opened a cleft above Lake Göscheneralp. It contained almost two tonnes of rock crystal.
88215.m: A huge crystal treasure was found on the Planggenstock in 2005.

a: A piece of frozen glacier ice
88216.e: Rock crystal is colourless, see-through quartz. It is the most common find of crystal hunters in the Alps.

88217.q: Roughly how long is the largest single crystal from the Planggenstock find?
88217.e: The middle crystal of the largest group measures about 107 cm. Such giant crystals only grow in large, undisturbed clefts.
88217.m: The largest Planggenstock crystals are about a metre long.

88218.q: What do crystal hunters need in many cantons before they are allowed to search for crystals?
88218.e: The cantons have their own rules for crystal hunting. You often need a licence or permit and must follow rules to protect nature.
88218.m: Crystal hunters often need a permit from the canton.

88219.q: Why is crystal hunting in the high mountains dangerous?
a: Because of falling rocks and the risk of falling
Because of the noise of the crystals
88219.e: Crystal hunters climb on steep, often crumbly rock. Loose stones and falls are the greatest dangers.
88219.m: Falling rocks and falls are risks in crystal hunting.

88220.q: Why do crystal hunters in the high mountains search mainly in summer and autumn?
a: Then the rock is usually free of snow
88220.e: In winter and spring there is a lot of snow in the mountains, and clefts are covered. Only in summer and autumn can you reach the rock.
88220.m: Crystal hunters are out mainly in summer and autumn.

88221.q: In which canton is the Lengenbach mineral quarry?
88221.e: The quarry is in the municipality of Binn in Upper Valais. It is one of the best-known mineral sites in the world.
88221.m: The Lengenbach quarry is in Valais.

88222.q: In which valley is the Lengenbach quarry?
88222.e: The valley is a side valley of the Goms and is now a regional nature park. It is famous among mineral collectors worldwide.
88222.m: The Lengenbach quarry is in the Binn valley.

88223.q: Where do the crystals grow in the Lengenbach quarry?
a: In the water of a mountain lake
In the ice of a glacier
88223.e: The finds sit in a white rock that looks like grains of sugar. In its hollows, the crystals had room to grow.
88223.m: The Lengenbach crystals grew in hollows in the rock.

88224.q: What is the Lengenbach quarry known for worldwide?
a: For many minerals discovered there for the first time
For the largest gold deposit in Europe
For the deepest cave in the Alps
88224.e: More than 40 kinds of minerals were described for the very first time at Lengenbach. Some are still not known from anywhere else.
88224.m: Many minerals were first discovered at Lengenbach.

88225.q: What is special about some minerals from the Lengenbach quarry?
a: They are not known from anywhere else in the world
They are made of pure gold
88225.e: At Lengenbach, for example, more than 30 rare thallium minerals are known, many of them only from here. This has made the site world-famous.
88225.m: Some minerals exist only at Lengenbach.

88226.q: What colour is the arsenic mineral realgar from the Lengenbach quarry?
88226.e: Realgar is a bright red arsenic sulphide. At Lengenbach it forms striking red bands in the pale rock.
88226.m: Realgar is a red arsenic mineral.

88227.q: Roughly how many different kinds of minerals are known from the Lengenbach quarry?
88227.e: A study in 2018 counted about 160 kinds of minerals from the quarry; today there are about 170. For such a small quarry, that is extraordinarily many.
88227.m: About 160 kinds of minerals are known from Lengenbach.

88228.q: What is the digging in the Lengenbach quarry for?
88228.e: Early mining in the 18th century hardly paid off. Since 1958, working groups have been recovering mineral specimens there without a break for science and collectors.
88228.m: At Lengenbach, minerals are sought for research and collections.

88229.q: What may visitors do at the “Klopfplatz” in front of the Lengenbach quarry?
88229.e: In summer, rock from the quarry is put out there. With a hammer and a magnifying glass you can search it yourself for small crystals.
88229.m: At the Klopfplatz you may search for minerals yourself.

88230.q: Between which atoms does an ionic bond typically form?
88230.e: Metal atoms give up electrons easily, and non-metal atoms take them in. The charged particles that form attract each other.
88230.m: An ionic bond usually joins a metal to a non-metal.

88231.q: Which force holds the oppositely charged ions together in an ionic bond?
88231.e: Positive and negative charges attract each other. This electrical attraction between the ions is the ionic bond.
88231.m: Opposite charges attract and hold ions together.

88232.q: What is a positively charged ion called?
88232.e: An atom that gives up electrons has more protons than electrons, so it is positively charged. In electrolysis, these ions move to the negative cathode.
88232.m: Positively charged ions are called cations.

88233.q: What is a negatively charged ion called?
88233.e: If an atom takes in extra electrons, it is negatively charged. In electrolysis, these ions move to the positive anode.
88233.m: Negatively charged ions are called anions.

88234.q: What charge does a magnesium atom get when it gives up its two outer electrons?
88234.e: Each electron given up takes a negative charge with it. After giving up two electrons, two positive charges are left over.
88234.m: Giving up electrons makes an atom positively charged.

88235.q: What is the charge of a sulphide ion, that is, a sulphur ion?
88235.e: A sulphur atom has six outer electrons and takes in two more. This gives it a double negative charge.
88235.m: Sulphur forms sulphide ions with a double negative charge.

88236.q: What is the regular arrangement of ions in a solid salt called?
88236.e: In a solid salt, the ions sit in turn in a regular pattern. This three-dimensional pattern is called an ionic lattice.
88236.m: Solid salts are made of a regular ionic lattice.

88237.q: Why do ionic compounds shatter when struck hard instead of changing shape?
a: Ions with the same charge end up side by side and repel each other
88237.e: If a blow shifts the layers of the lattice, ions with the same charge are suddenly next to each other. They repel each other and the crystal breaks.
88237.m: Ionic crystals are brittle because like charges repel.

88238.q: What is the formula of magnesium oxide, a compound of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻?
88238.e: The two positive charges of the magnesium ion exactly balance the two negative charges of the oxide ion. That is why the ions are in a ratio of 1 to 1.
88238.m: In an ionic compound the charges balance overall.

88239.q: How does a covalent bond form?
a: Two atoms share a pair of electrons
One atom gives another an electron
Metal atoms form an electron gas
88239.e: In a covalent bond, electrons belong to both atoms together. Each atom usually adds one electron to the shared pair.
88239.m: In a covalent bond, atoms share electrons.

88241.q: Between which atoms do covalent bonds typically occur?
a: Between metal and noble gas atoms
88241.e: Non-metal atoms all attract electrons fairly strongly. None of them gives up its electrons completely, so they share them.
88241.m: Non-metals usually join each other with covalent bonds.

88242.q: How many shared pairs of electrons does a double bond have?
88242.e: In a double bond, two atoms share two pairs of electrons, so four electrons in total.
88242.m: A double bond is made of two shared pairs of electrons.

88243.q: Which bond joins the two atoms in the oxygen molecule O₂?
88243.e: Each oxygen atom has six outer electrons and needs two more. That is why the two atoms share two pairs of electrons.
88243.m: In the oxygen molecule the atoms are joined by a double bond.

88244.q: What kind of particle forms when a few non-metal atoms join through covalent bonds?
88244.e: Atoms joined by covalent bonds form a closed unit such as H₂O or CO₂. These units are called molecules.
88244.m: Covalent bonds hold the atoms together in molecules.

88245.q: What is a covalent bond with three shared pairs of electrons called?
88245.e: A triple bond is very strong. It is found, for example, in the nitrogen molecule N₂.
88245.m: Three shared pairs of electrons make a triple bond.

88246.q: How many covalent bonds does a hydrogen atom form?
88246.e: Hydrogen has only one electron. With one shared pair of electrons, its shell is already full.
88246.m: A hydrogen atom always forms just one bond.

88247.q: In which substance are all the atoms joined by covalent bonds into a giant lattice?
88247.e: In diamond, every carbon atom is firmly joined to four neighbours. This continuous lattice of atoms makes it extremely hard.
88247.m: Diamond is a giant lattice of covalent bonds.

88248.q: What is the model called that describes the freely moving electrons in a metal?
88248.e: The outer electrons of the metal atoms do not belong to any one atom. They move like a gas between the positively charged metal particles.
88248.m: In a metal, the outer electrons move like an electron gas.

88249.e: Electric current is flowing charge. When a voltage is applied, the mobile electrons in the metal can easily move in one direction.
88249.m: Metals conduct electricity thanks to their mobile electrons.

88250.q: Why can metals be hammered and bent without breaking?
a: The layers of metal slide past each other without the bond breaking
Metals contain a lot of air
88250.e: The mobile electrons hold the metal particles together even after they have shifted. So the metal changes shape instead of breaking.
88250.m: Metals can be shaped because the metallic bond survives the shift.

88251.q: Which property of a metal's surface is also explained by the freely moving electrons?
88251.e: The mobile electrons at the surface reflect almost all the light that hits them. That is why freshly polished metals shine.
88251.m: Metals shine because their electrons reflect the light.

88252.q: What is a mixture of two or more metals, such as bronze, called?
88252.e: Melting metals together makes a new metal mixture with different properties. Bronze is often harder than its ingredients.
88252.m: A mixture of metals is called an alloy.

88253.q: Which metals is brass made of?
88253.e: Brass is a golden yellow alloy of copper and zinc. It is used, for example, for door handles and brass instruments.
88253.m: Brass is made from copper and zinc.

88254.q: Why are metals especially good at conducting heat?
a: The mobile electrons pass on energy quickly
88254.e: The freely moving electrons take in movement energy and carry it quickly through the whole metal. That is why a metal spoon in tea soon gets hot.
88254.m: Metals conduct heat well because their electrons carry energy.

88255.q: What are the positively charged particles called that remain in the metal lattice when the outer electrons are set free?
88255.e: When a metal atom gives its outer electrons to the shared electron gas, the rest of the atom is left with a positive charge. This remainder is called an atomic core.
88255.m: In a metal lattice, positive atomic cores sit in an electron gas.

88256.q: Which particles is a salt made of?
88256.e: In salts, positively and negatively charged particles take turns. Overall a salt is electrically neutral.
88256.m: Salts are made of cations and anions.

88257.q: What is the salt with the formula MgSO₄, also known as Epsom salt?
88257.e: Mg stands for magnesium and SO₄ for the sulphate group. The salt tastes bitter and is used, for example, in bath salts.

88258.q: Which salt is the main ingredient of gypsum?
88258.e: Gypsum is calcium sulphate with built-in water of crystallisation. It is used for walls, plaster casts and models.
88258.m: Gypsum is made of calcium sulphate.

88259.q: Why do salts usually have very high melting points?
a: The attraction between the ions is very strong
Salts contain a lot of water
Salts are made of light gases
88259.e: To melt a salt, you have to overcome the strong attraction in the ionic lattice. That needs a lot of energy and high temperatures.
88259.m: Salts only melt at high temperatures.

88260.q: What are the salts of hydrochloric acid called?
88260.e: Hydrochloric acid is a solution of hydrogen chloride (HCl). Its acid group is the chloride ion Cl⁻.
88260.m: The salts of hydrochloric acid are called chlorides.

88261.q: What are the salts of sulphuric acid called?
88261.e: The acid group of sulphuric acid is the sulphate ion. One example is copper sulphate.
88261.m: The salts of sulphuric acid are called sulphates.

88262.q: Which salt is often used as a fertiliser because it gives plants potassium?
88262.e: Plants need potassium as an important nutrient. Potassium chloride is mined for this and sold as potash fertiliser.
88262.m: Potassium chloride is an important potash fertiliser.

88263.q: What colour are copper sulphate crystals that contain water of crystallisation?
88263.e: Copper sulphate with water of crystallisation forms bright blue crystals. Without water, the salt is white.
88263.m: Copper sulphate containing water is blue.

88264.q: What is sodium chloride called in everyday life?
88264.e: Sodium chloride is the salt we use to season food. It is called table salt or cooking salt.
88264.m: Sodium chloride is our table salt.

88265.q: What happens to table salt in a hot frying pan?
88265.e: Table salt only melts at very high temperatures of about 800 degrees. So in the pan it stays solid.
88265.m: Table salt only melts at very high temperatures.

88266.q: What shape are table salt crystals under a magnifying glass?
88266.e: The ions in table salt are arranged in a regular, cube-shaped lattice. That is why the crystals look like little cubes.

88267.q: In what ratio are sodium and chloride ions found in table salt?
88267.e: A sodium ion has a single positive charge, a chloride ion a single negative charge. For the crystal to be neutral, there must be equal numbers of both.
88267.m: Table salt contains as many sodium ions as chloride ions.

88268.q: Why is it easier to float in the very salty Dead Sea than in a lake?
a: The salt water has a higher density
There are waves in the Dead Sea
88268.e: Dissolved salt makes water denser. Denser water holds the body up better, so you float almost by yourself.
88268.m: Salt water holds you up better because it is denser.

88269.q: What happens if you throw a piece of pure sodium into water?
a: It reacts violently and hydrogen forms
It simply sinks to the bottom
88269.e: Sodium is a very reactive alkali metal. With water it forms sodium hydroxide solution and hydrogen gas, often with hissing and sometimes even with fire.
88269.m: Pure sodium reacts violently with water.

88270.q: What is the most salt per day that the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends for adults?
88270.e: The WHO recommends that adults eat less than 5 grams of salt per day, about one teaspoon. Too much salt can raise blood pressure.
88270.m: Adults should eat less than 5 grams of salt per day.

88271.q: What happens to the ions when table salt dissolves in water?
a: They are surrounded by water molecules and spread out
They join up to form molecules
They break down into protons and neutrons
88271.e: The water molecules pull the ions out of the lattice and gather around them. This process is called hydration.
88271.m: When salt dissolves, the ions are surrounded by water molecules.

88272.q: What is left when salt water evaporates completely?
88272.e: When it evaporates, only the water escapes. The dissolved salt is left behind as crystals. This is how sea salt is made.
88272.m: When salt water evaporates, the salt is left behind.

88273.q: What does the electronegativity of an atom describe?
a: How strongly it attracts electrons in a bond
How many protons it has in its nucleus
88273.e: Electronegativity is a measure of how strongly an atom pulls the shared pair of electrons in a bond towards itself.
88273.m: Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom attracts bonding electrons.

88274.q: What does it mean if an atom has a high electronegativity?
a: It has a great many neutrons
88274.e: Electronegativity tells you how strongly an atom pulls the electrons in a bond towards itself. The higher the value, the stronger the pull.
88274.m: High electronegativity means a strong pull on bonding electrons.

88279.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity of all?
88279.e: Fluorine attracts electrons in a bond more strongly than any other element. It is at the top right of the periodic table.
88279.m: Fluorine is the most electronegative element.

88280.q: What is the difference in electronegativity in a bond between two identical atoms, for example in H₂?
88280.e: Two identical atoms have exactly the same electronegativity. So the difference is zero, and the pair of electrons sits exactly in the middle.
88280.m: Identical atoms pull the bonding pair equally strongly.

88281.q: What does a molecular formula tell you?
a: Which atoms and how many of each are in a molecule
How the atoms are arranged in space
How heavy a kilogram of the substance is
At what temperature the substance boils
88281.e: The molecular formula lists all the atoms in a molecule, for example H₂O. It says nothing about how the atoms are linked.
88281.m: The molecular formula counts the atoms in a molecule.

88282.q: What is the molecular formula of methane, the main part of natural gas?
88282.e: A methane molecule is made of one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. It is the simplest hydrocarbon.

88283.q: How many atoms are in one molecule of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆)?
88283.e: You count 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 6 oxygen atoms. 6 + 12 + 6 makes 24 atoms.
88283.m: Adding up the numbers in the molecular formula gives the number of atoms.

88284.q: What is the molecular formula of ammonia?
88284.e: An ammonia molecule is made of one nitrogen atom and three hydrogen atoms. It has a sharp smell and is used for fertiliser.

88285.q: Which substance has the molecular formula C₂H₆O?
88285.e: Ethanol, the alcohol in drinks, is made of 2 carbon, 6 hydrogen and one oxygen atom. It is found in wine and beer.
88285.m: The alcohol in drinks has the molecular formula C₂H₆O.

88286.q: How many atoms in total are in one molecule of sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄)?
88286.e: H₂SO₄ contains 2 hydrogen atoms, 1 sulphur atom and 4 oxygen atoms. 2 + 1 + 4 makes 7.
88286.m: No number after a symbol means one atom.

88287.q: What is the formula of carbon dioxide?
88287.e: Carbon dioxide has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. The prefix ‘di’ means two.
88287.m: Carbon dioxide has the formula CO₂.

88288.q: What does the small 2 in the formula H₂O mean?
a: A molecule contains two hydrogen atoms
The molecule has a double charge
88288.e: The small number applies to the symbol directly in front of it. So a water molecule has two H atoms and one O atom.
88288.m: Small numbers count the atoms of the symbol in front.

88290.q: What does a structural formula show in addition to the molecular formula?
a: How the atoms are joined to each other
How many neutrons the atoms have
88290.e: In the structural formula you can see which atom is bonded to which. This lets you tell apart substances with the same molecular formula.
88290.m: The structural formula shows how the atoms are linked.

88291.q: What does a line between two atoms in a structural formula mean?
88291.e: In the structural formula, each line stands for a shared pair of electrons, that is, a bond. This shows which atoms are joined.
88291.m: A line in a structural formula is a bond.

88292.q: How many bond lines does the structural formula of ethane (C₂H₆) show?
88292.e: Each of the six hydrogen atoms is attached to a carbon atom by a line. There is also a line between the two carbon atoms: 6 + 1 makes 7.
88292.m: In a structural formula, each line stands for a single bond.

88293.q: What is the structural formula of carbon dioxide?
88293.e: The carbon atom sits in the middle and has a double bond to each oxygen atom. The molecule is straight.
88293.m: In carbon dioxide, the carbon is in the middle.

88294.q: What shape is a water molecule?
88294.e: The two lone pairs of electrons on the oxygen push the two hydrogen atoms together. That is why the molecule is bent like a V.

88295.q: How many bond lines come from each carbon atom in a structural formula?
88295.e: Carbon has four outer electrons, so it forms four bonds. A double bond counts as two lines.
88295.m: Carbon always has four bonds in structural formulas.

88296.q: Which molecular formula belongs to the structural formula H-O-O-H?
88296.e: You count two hydrogen and two oxygen atoms. The substance is called hydrogen peroxide and is used for bleaching.
88296.m: You can count the molecular formula from the structural formula.

88298.q: Where do hydrogen bonds act in liquid water?
a: Between the water and the air
88298.e: A hydrogen atom of one molecule is attracted by the oxygen atom of a neighbouring molecule. That way the molecules loosely cling together.
88298.m: Hydrogen bonds link water molecules to each other.

88299.q: What is the weak attraction called that makes water molecules stick to each other?
88299.e: The hydrogen atom of one water molecule is attracted by the oxygen atom of a neighbouring molecule. This attraction is called a hydrogen bond.
88299.m: Water molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds.

88300.q: Why does ice float on liquid water?
a: In ice, hydrogen bonds hold the molecules further apart
Ice contains trapped bubbles of nitrogen
Ice is repelled magnetically by water
88300.e: When water freezes, the hydrogen bonds arrange the molecules into an open lattice with gaps. That is why ice has a lower density than water.
88300.m: Ice is lighter than water because its lattice has gaps.

88301.q: At what temperature does water have its greatest density?
88301.e: Water is densest at around 4 °C. That is why in winter water at 4 degrees gathers at the bottom of lakes, and fish survive there.

88302.q: What holds the two strands of DNA together?
88302.e: The bases of the two strands face each other in pairs and are joined by two or three hydrogen bonds. This allows the DNA to be separated for copying.
88302.m: Hydrogen bonds hold the DNA double helix together.

88303.q: How strong is a hydrogen bond compared with a covalent bond?
88303.e: A hydrogen bond is an attraction between molecules and is only a small fraction as strong as a covalent bond. That is why it is easy to break.
88303.m: Hydrogen bonds are much weaker than covalent bonds.

88304.q: Why can pond skaters walk on the surface of water?
a: Hydrogen bonds create a high surface tension
The water is frozen at the surface
The insects are lighter than air
There is low pressure under the surface
88304.e: At the surface, the water molecules pull strongly together through hydrogen bonds. This forms a kind of thin skin that can carry small animals.
88304.m: Hydrogen bonds give water a high surface tension.

88305.q: What happens to the hydrogen bonds when water boils?
88305.e: When water boils, the molecules get so much energy that the hydrogen bonds break. The molecules separate and fly off as steam.
88305.m: When water boils, the hydrogen bonds between the molecules break.

a: A molecule with a positive end and a negative end
A molecule made of exactly two atoms
A molecule that is always a gas
88306.e: If one atom attracts the bonding electrons more strongly, a negative part forms there. If the centres of charge are apart, the molecule has two poles.
88306.m: A dipole has a positive end and a negative end.

88307.q: Which well-known molecule is a dipole?
88307.e: In the water molecule, oxygen attracts the electrons more strongly than hydrogen. Molecules made of two identical atoms have no poles.

88308.q: Which simple experiment shows that water is made of dipole molecules?
a: A thin stream of water is bent by a rubbed plastic rod
Water gets cold in the fridge
An ice cube melts in your hand
88308.e: The rubbed rod is electrically charged. The water molecules turn the matching end towards it, and the stream bends.
88308.m: A charged rod bends a stream of water.

88309.q: Which end of a water molecule is partly negatively charged?
88309.e: Oxygen attracts the bonding electrons more strongly than hydrogen. That is why there is a partial negative charge on the oxygen.
88309.m: In the water molecule, oxygen is the negative pole.

88311.q: Why do oil and water not mix?
a: Water is polar, oil is non-polar
Water is always colder than oil
88311.e: Because of their poles, water molecules cling tightly together and do not let the non-polar oil molecules in between. The rule is: like dissolves like.
88311.m: Polar and non-polar substances do not mix well.

88312.q: What does the prefix ‘di’ in the word dipole mean?
88312.e: ‘Di’ comes from Greek and means two. So a dipole has two poles.
88312.m: A dipole is a particle with two poles.

88313.q: What are substances called that mix well with water or dissolve in it?
88313.e: Hydrophilic means ‘water-loving’. Such substances are usually polar and are surrounded well by water molecules.

88314.q: How many electrons does a nitrogen atom share with bonding partners to reach the octet?
88314.e: Nitrogen has five outer electrons and needs three more. That is why it forms three bonds in molecules such as NH₃.

88315.q: How many electrons does an oxygen atom take in to get a full outer shell?
88315.e: Oxygen has six outer electrons. With two extra electrons it reaches eight, the same arrangement as the noble gas neon.
88315.m: Oxygen needs two electrons for a full octet.

88316.q: How many electrons does a sodium atom give up to reach the electron arrangement of a noble gas?
88316.e: Sodium has only one electron in its outermost shell. If it gives this up, the full shell underneath becomes the new outer shell.
88316.m: Sodium gives up one electron and so becomes stable.

88317.q: Which element is an exception and aims for only two electrons in its outer shell?
88317.e: Hydrogen has only the first shell, and only two electrons fit into it. With two it reaches the arrangement of helium.
88317.m: Hydrogen is already happy with two electrons.

88318.q: How many electrons does a calcium atom give up to reach the electron arrangement of a noble gas?
88318.e: Calcium has two electrons in its outermost shell. If it gives up both, the ion Ca²⁺ forms, with the arrangement of argon.
88318.m: Calcium becomes an ion with a double positive charge.

88319.q: According to the octet rule, how many electrons do most atoms want in their outermost shell?
88319.e: ‘Octet’ means a group of eight. With eight outer electrons, atoms have a stable arrangement like the noble gases.
88319.m: Most atoms aim for eight outer electrons.

88320.q: Which noble gas has the same electron arrangement as the chloride ion Cl⁻?
88320.e: The chloride ion has 18 electrons. The noble gas that comes directly after chlorine in the periodic table has exactly as many.
88320.m: Ions often reach the electron arrangement of a noble gas.

88321.q: How can you tell the number of outer electrons of a main group element from the periodic table?
a: From the number of the main group
From the number of the period
From the colour of the box
88321.e: All elements in a main group have the same number of outer electrons. Carbon is in main group 4 and has four.
88321.m: The main group number shows the number of outer electrons.

88322.q: What do you draw as dots or lines around the element symbol in a Lewis formula?
88322.e: The Lewis formula shows the outer electrons, also called valence electrons. A dot is one electron, a line is a pair of electrons.
88322.m: The Lewis formula shows an atom's outer electrons.

88323.q: How many electrons does a single line in a Lewis formula stand for?
88323.e: A line stands for a pair of electrons. A single electron, on the other hand, is drawn as a dot.
88323.m: A line in a Lewis formula stands for two electrons.

88324.q: How many lone pairs of electrons does the oxygen atom in a water molecule have?
88324.e: Oxygen has six valence electrons. It uses two of them for the bonds to the H atoms, and the other four form two lone pairs.
88324.m: The oxygen in water carries two lone pairs of electrons.

88325.q: How many lone pairs of electrons does the nitrogen atom in an ammonia molecule have?
88325.e: Nitrogen has five valence electrons. It needs three for the bonds to the H atoms, and the remaining two form a lone pair.
88325.m: In ammonia, the nitrogen has one lone pair of electrons.

88326.q: How many lone pairs of electrons does each atom in the chlorine molecule Cl₂ carry?
88326.e: Each chlorine atom has seven valence electrons. One goes into the shared bond, and the other six form three lone pairs.
88326.m: Each chlorine atom in Cl₂ has three lone pairs of electrons.

88327.q: How many valence electrons must you share out in total in the Lewis formula of methane (CH₄)?
88327.e: Carbon brings four, and the four hydrogen atoms bring one each. 4 + 4 makes 8 electrons, so four bond lines.
88327.m: For a Lewis formula, first add up all the valence electrons.

88328.q: What other name is the Lewis formula known by?
88328.e: Because it shows the valence electrons as dots or as lines for pairs, it is also called an electron dot formula or electron formula.
88328.m: The Lewis formula is also called the electron dot formula.

88329.q: What does a Lewis formula show in addition to a simple structural formula?
a: The number of neutrons in the nucleus
88329.e: In a Lewis formula you draw the non-bonding electron pairs as well as the bonds. That way you can see, for example, the two lone pairs on the oxygen in water.
88329.m: A Lewis formula also shows the lone pairs of electrons.

a: It sets which number stands for which character
It connects the computer to the internet
88528.e: ASCII is an American standard. Every letter, digit and punctuation mark gets a number so that the computer can store text.
88528.m: ASCII is an old American standard for encoding characters.

88529.q: In ASCII code, “A” has the code 65 and “B” has the code 66. What code does “D” have?
88529.e: In ASCII the capital letters follow each other directly: A = 65, B = 66, C = 67, D = 68.
88529.m: In ASCII code every letter is a number.

88530.q: In ASCII code, the digit “0” has the code 48. What code does the digit “3” have?
88530.e: The digits 0 to 9 have the codes 48 to 57. So the digit 3 has 48 + 3 = 51. For the computer, the character “3” is not the same as the number 3.
88530.m: A digit as a character has a different code from its number value.

88531.q: In ASCII code, “A” has the code 65 and “a” has the code 97. By how much do the two codes differ?
88531.e: 97 minus 65 is 32. This gap applies to all letters; for example, “B” has the code 66 and “b” the code 98.
88531.m: In ASCII, small letters always have a code 32 higher than capital letters.

88532.q: Does the space have its own number in ASCII code?
a: Yes, the space has its own code too
No, it is left out when saving
No, it is saved as the letter A
88532.e: The space has the number 32 in ASCII code. For the computer it is a character like any other.
88532.m: Even a space is a character with its own code for the computer.

88533.q: Roughly when was ASCII code created?
88533.e: The first version of ASCII appeared in 1963 in the USA, in the early days of computers. It was revised several times later.
88533.m: ASCII dates from the early sixties.

88534.q: Which character is not included in the original ASCII code?
88534.e: ASCII only contains the English letters, without umlauts. For “ä”, “ö” and “ü” other codes were needed later.
88534.m: German umlauts are missing from the original ASCII code.

88535.q: What are invisible ASCII characters like the line break or the tab called?
88535.e: Control characters are commands such as a line break or a tab. You do not see them as characters on the screen. In ASCII code they have the numbers 0 to 31.
88535.m: Control characters are invisible commands such as a line break.

88536.q: In ASCII code “A” = 65 and “a” = 97. Which word do the codes 72 and 105 make?
88536.e: 72 is 65 + 7, so the eighth capital letter, H. 105 is 97 + 8, so the ninth small letter, i. Together they make “Hi”.
88536.m: With an ASCII table you can turn sequences of numbers back into text.

88537.q: What is the aim of Unicode?
a: To give every written character in the world a code
To make pictures smaller without loss
88537.e: Unicode is meant to cover all the scripts in the world, from Latin to Arabic to Chinese. This means texts can be exchanged in any language.
88537.m: Unicode is a shared character code for all the languages of the world.

88538.q: What does every character get in Unicode?
88538.e: Every character, whether a letter, a digit or an emoji, has its own number in Unicode. This way every computer knows which character is meant.
88538.m: In Unicode every character has its own number.

88539.q: Which popular picture symbols are also part of the Unicode standard?
88539.e: Emojis are characters defined in the Unicode standard. That is why you can send them between different devices.
88539.m: Emojis are characters from the Unicode standard.

88540.q: Roughly how many characters does Unicode include (as of 2025)?
88540.e: Characters are added with every new version. Version 17.0 from 2025 contains about 160,000 characters.
88540.m: Unicode keeps growing with every new version.

88541.q: Which characters make up the first 128 code points of Unicode?
a: The same characters as in ASCII code
88541.e: Unicode was built so that the first 128 characters match ASCII. This keeps old texts readable.
88541.m: Unicode is backwards compatible with the old ASCII code.

88542.q: What do you often see when a text is opened with the wrong character encoding?
a: A strange jumble of characters instead of umlauts
88542.e: If UTF-8 is read wrongly, for example, something like “Ã¤” appears instead of “ä”. The bytes are then matched to other characters.
88542.m: A jumble of characters appears when sender and receiver use different encodings.

a: An encoding that stores Unicode characters as bytes
88543.e: UTF-8 sets how Unicode characters are stored in bytes. Today it is the most common encoding on the internet.
88543.m: UTF-8 is the most common way of storing Unicode texts.

88544.q: Which organisation looks after the Unicode standard?
88544.e: The Unicode Consortium is a non-profit organisation. For example, it decides which new emojis are added.
88544.m: The Unicode Consortium decides on new Unicode characters.

88545.q: What base does the hexadecimal system have?
88545.e: “Hexadecimal” means sixteen. So you need sixteen different digits.
88545.m: The hexadecimal system is a place value system with sixteen digits.

88546.q: What value does the hexadecimal digit F have?
88546.e: After 0 to 9 come A = 10, B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14 and F = 15.
88546.m: In the hexadecimal system the letters A to F stand for the values ten to fifteen.

88547.q: Which decimal number matches the hexadecimal number 1F?
88547.m: In hexadecimal numbers, every place is worth sixteen times as much as the place to its right.

88548.q: How do you write the decimal number 255 in the hexadecimal system?
88548.e: FF means 15·16 + 15 = 255. That is the largest two-digit hexadecimal number.
88548.m: With two hexadecimal digits you can write values from zero to two hundred and fifty-five.

88549.q: What colour does the web colour code #FF0000 have?
88549.e: A colour code consists of three pairs for red, green and blue. With #FF0000 red is fully on, and green and blue are 00.
88549.m: Web colours are given with three hexadecimal pairs for red, green and blue.

88550.q: How many bits can you represent with a single hexadecimal digit?
88550.e: A hexadecimal digit has 16 values, and 16 = 2·2·2·2. So it matches exactly 4 bits.
88550.m: One hexadecimal digit replaces exactly four binary places.

88551.q: Which decimal number matches the hexadecimal number 10?
88551.e: The 1 is in the sixteens place, the 0 in the ones place: 1·16 + 0 = 16.
88551.m: The hexadecimal number one zero has the value sixteen.

88552.q: Which decimal number matches the hexadecimal number 2A?
88552.m: To convert a hexadecimal number, you multiply each digit by its place value.

88553.q: Which hexadecimal number comes directly after 9F?
88553.e: After F (15) there is a carry: the ones place becomes 0 and the sixteens place jumps from 9 to A.
88553.m: After the digit F there is a carry in the hexadecimal system.

88554.q: What is the idea behind run-length encoding?
a: Identical characters in a row are stored as a count and the character
Common words are replaced by pictures
Every second character is left out
88554.e: Instead of “AAAAA” you store, for example, “5A”. Long repetitions take up much less space this way.
88554.m: Run-length encoding groups together identical characters in a row.

88555.q: What is “AAAABBBCCD” in run-length encoding (count before the character)?
88555.e: There are 4 A, 3 B, 2 C and 1 D. This becomes 4A3B2C1D.
88555.m: You count how many times a character appears in a row and write the count next to it.

88556.q: What does the abbreviation RLE stand for?
88556.e: RLE stands for run-length encoding. “Run” here means a sequence of identical values.
88556.m: Run-length encoding is often abbreviated to RLE.

88557.q: Is information lost with run-length encoding?
88557.e: From “4A” you can get back “AAAA” exactly. So the original can be fully restored.
88557.m: With lossless compression you get the original back exactly.

88558.q: Which pictures is run-length encoding especially good for?
a: Pictures with large areas of one colour
Pictures where every pixel is different
88558.e: Large areas of the same colour have long rows of identical pixels. These can be described very briefly.
88558.m: The more identical values lie next to each other, the better run-length encoding works.

88559.q: How many characters long does “ABABAB” (6 characters) become with run-length encoding in the form count plus character?
88559.e: There are no repetitions, so every character becomes “1A” or “1B”. 6 characters become 12.
88559.m: Without repetitions, run-length encoding can even make a file bigger.

88560.q: Which row of pixels does “3W2B1W” give, if W stands for white and B for black?
88560.e: 3W means three white pixels, 2B two black and 1W one white pixel: WWWBBW.
88560.m: When unpacking, you write each character as many times as the number in front of it says.

88561.q: How do you write a row of 10 white, 2 black and 10 white pixels in run-length encoding?
88561.e: The three sections are written down in order as count and colour: 10W, 2B, 10W.
88561.m: In run-length encoding the order of the sections is kept.

88562.q: Which device used run-length encoding for black and white pages for a long time?
88562.e: A typical page of writing has a lot of white. That is why fax machines send how long the white and black sections of each line are.
88562.m: Fax machines save transmission time by grouping together long white sections.

88563.q: What is a parity bit for?
88563.e: The parity bit is added to data. The receiver can use it to check whether a bit has flipped along the way.
88563.m: A parity bit is a simple check bit against transmission errors.

88564.q: Which parity bit is added to 1011001 with even parity?
88564.e: 1011001 contains four ones, which is already an even number. So the parity bit is 0.
88564.m: With even parity, the parity bit makes the number of ones even.

88565.q: Which parity bit is added to 1101000 with even parity?
88565.e: 1101000 contains three ones. With a parity bit of 1 there are four, an even number.
88565.m: If the number of ones is odd, the even parity bit is a one.

88566.q: Which parity bit is added to 1100110 with odd parity?
88566.e: 1100110 contains four ones. For the number to be odd, the parity bit must be 1.
88566.m: With odd parity the total number of ones must be odd.

88567.q: Which error can a single parity bit not detect?
a: When two bits flip at the same time
88567.e: If two bits flip, the number of ones stays even or odd as before. The check then reports no error.
88567.m: A parity bit only detects an odd number of bit errors.

88568.q: Can a simple parity bit also correct an error?
a: No, it does not show which bit is wrong
Yes, if the data is short
88568.e: The parity bit only shows that something is wrong, not where. The data then has to be sent again.
88568.m: A parity bit detects errors but does not correct them.

88569.q: With even parity, a receiver gets 10110110 (including the parity bit). What follows from this?
88569.e: 10110110 contains five ones. With even parity the number should be even, so something has gone wrong.
88569.m: If the parity does not match at the receiver, at least one bit has been changed.

88570.q: A parity bit is added to 7 data bits. How many bits are then sent?
88570.e: 1 parity bit is added to the 7 data bits. Together that makes 8 bits, exactly one byte.
88570.m: The parity bit is sent along with the data.

88571.q: What is a graphic called that is stored as a grid of individual coloured dots?
88571.e: A raster graphic stores a colour for each dot (pixel) in the grid.
88571.m: A raster graphic is a mosaic of many pixels.

88572.q: What happens when you enlarge a raster graphic a lot?
88572.e: When you enlarge it, the individual pixels are simply shown bigger. Slanted edges then look like steps.
88572.m: Raster graphics lose sharpness when enlarged a lot.

88573.q: Which of these file formats stores a raster graphic?
88573.e: PNG stores pictures pixel by pixel. SVG is a vector format, TXT and HTML are text formats.
88573.m: PNG is a common format for raster graphics.

88574.q: How much memory does an uncompressed picture with 100 × 100 pixels and 24-bit colour depth need?
88574.e: 100 · 100 = 10,000 pixels. Each pixel needs 24 bits, which is 3 bytes: 10,000 · 3 = 30,000 bytes.
88574.m: The memory a raster graphic needs grows with the number of pixels and the colour depth.

88575.q: How many colours can a pixel with 1-bit colour depth show?
88575.e: A bit can only be 0 or 1. So a picture like this has only two colours, usually black and white.
88575.m: With one bit per pixel you get a pure black and white picture.

88576.q: What is the minimum colour depth in bits a pixel needs so that a picture can have 16 different colours?
88576.e: With n bits there are 2^n possibilities. 2^4 = 16, so 4 bits are enough.
88576.m: With every extra bit of colour depth, the number of possible colours doubles.

88577.q: What kind of program is typically used to edit photos and other raster graphics?
88577.e: Image editing programs change individual pixels, for example when brightening or retouching a photo.
88577.m: You edit photos with programs that can change individual pixels.

88578.q: What kind of graphic does a digital camera produce?
88578.e: The camera's image sensor measures the brightness and colour for every dot. This creates a grid of pixels.
88578.m: Digital photos are always made of pixels.

88579.q: What does a vector graphic consist of?
a: Geometric shapes such as lines, circles and curves
88579.e: A vector graphic stores shapes with coordinates and properties, such as “circle with centre and radius”.
88579.m: A vector graphic describes a picture with mathematical shapes.

88580.q: What happens when you enlarge a vector graphic a lot?
88580.e: The shapes are recalculated at every size. That is why edges always stay smooth.
88580.m: Vector graphics can be enlarged without losing quality.

88581.q: What are vector graphics especially good for?
88581.e: Logos consist of clear shapes and a few areas of colour. Shapes like these are easy to describe mathematically.
88581.m: Logos and pictograms are usually designed as vector graphics.

88582.q: Why are vector graphics not well suited to photos?
a: Photos have countless fine colour gradients
Photos are always black and white
88582.e: A photo contains millions of slightly different coloured dots. Describing these as shapes would be extremely complicated.
88582.m: For photos with many colour gradients, raster graphics are better suited.

88583.q: What does the abbreviation SVG stand for?
88583.e: SVG means a vector graphic that can be scaled. The format is often used on websites for symbols.
88583.m: SVG is a common vector format for the web.

88584.q: How does a vector program store a curved line?
a: With a few points from which the curve is calculated
As a photo of the line
88584.e: A vector graphic only remembers start, end and control points. From these the program recalculates the curve at every size.
88584.m: Vector programs calculate curves from a few points.

88585.q: Why do letters on the screen stay sharp even in large type?
a: Fonts are stored as vector outlines
The screen has extra letter pixels
The font is photographed again each time
88585.e: Modern fonts store the outlines of the letters as curves. They are recalculated for every size.
88585.m: Computer fonts consist of described outlines and not of fixed pixels.

88586.q: What is converting a vector graphic into pixels for display called?
88586.e: Screens are made of pixels. Rasterisation works out which pixels a shape covers.
88586.m: Every vector graphic has to be converted into pixels for the screen.

88587.q: How many pixels does a Full HD picture with 1920 × 1080 pixels have?
88587.m: The number of pixels in a picture is width times height.

88588.q: What resolution does a picture in 4K UHD have?
88588.e: 4K UHD has twice as many pixels in width and in height as Full HD, so four times as many pixels.
88588.m: Ultra HD has four times as many pixels as Full HD.

88589.q: What does the abbreviation dpi stand for?
88589.e: dpi tells you how many dots are printed or scanned per inch (2.54 cm).
88589.m: The dpi figure describes the density of dots when printing or scanning.

88590.q: Which resolution is a usual guideline for a good-quality photo print?
88590.e: At about 300 dots per inch, the eye no longer sees individual dots from a normal distance.
88590.m: For good photo prints you need a high dot density.

88591.q: How many pixels does a photo with 4000 × 3000 pixels have?
88591.m: Width times height gives the total number of dots in a picture.

88592.q: What does a higher resolution do for a photo?
a: More detail, but a bigger file
Less detail and a smaller file
More colours, but the same number of pixels
88592.e: More pixels can show finer details. But every pixel needs memory, so the file gets bigger.
88592.m: A higher resolution shows more detail and needs more storage space.

88593.q: What does “megapixels” mean for a camera?
88593.e: Mega means million. A camera with 20 megapixels takes pictures with about 20 million pixels.
88593.m: Megapixels tell you how many millions of dots a photo consists of.

88594.q: A picture is 1200 pixels wide. Roughly how wide will it be if you print it at 300 dpi?
88594.e: 1200 : 300 = 4 inches. One inch measures 2.54 cm, so it is about 10 cm.
88594.m: The print size depends on the number of pixels and the chosen dot density.

88595.q: How many bytes are in a kilobyte according to the International System of Units (SI)?
88595.e: The prefix “kilo” means thousand, as in kilometre or kilogram.
88595.m: According to the system of units, a kilobyte is a thousand bytes.

88596.q: How many bytes are in a megabyte according to the International System of Units?
88596.e: Mega means million. So a megabyte is 1000 kilobytes or 1,000,000 bytes.
88596.m: A megabyte is a thousand kilobytes.

88597.q: How much memory does a text with 2000 characters need if each character takes up 1 byte?
88597.e: 2000 characters · 1 byte = 2000 bytes, which is 2 kilobytes.
88597.m: Plain texts need very little storage space.

88598.q: Why does a computer often show a 500 GB hard drive as only about 465 “GB”?
a: The rest is taken up by viruses
88598.e: The manufacturer calculates with 1000 per step, some operating systems with 1024. 500,000,000,000 bytes divided by 1024³ gives about 465.
88598.m: Different conversions lead to different storage figures.

88599.q: Roughly how many photos of 2 megabytes each fit into 1 gigabyte of storage?
88599.m: A gigabyte is a thousand megabytes.

88600.q: Which unit lies in size between kilobyte and gigabyte?
88600.e: The order is byte, kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte. Each step is about a thousand times bigger.
88600.m: Storage units go up in steps of about a thousand.

88601.q: Which file is usually the smallest?
a: A piece of music as an MP3
88601.e: A short text file usually needs only a few kilobytes. Photos and music need megabytes, films even gigabytes.
88601.m: Texts are very small compared with pictures, music and films.

88602.q: In which unit is the speed of an internet connection usually given?
88602.e: Transfer rates are usually given in bits per second, such as 100 Mbit/s. Storage sizes, on the other hand, are given in bytes.
88602.m: Data rates are usually measured in bits per second, but storage in bytes.

88603.q: An audio CD has a sampling rate of 44,100 Hz. What does that mean?
a: The sound is measured 44,100 times per second
The CD spins 44,100 times per minute
88603.e: Hertz means “per second”. The audio CD stores 44,100 measurements per second for each channel.
88603.m: The audio CD works with forty-four thousand one hundred measurements per second.

88604.q: What does the sampling rate tell you about digital sound?
a: How many measurements are recorded per second
88604.e: A microphone delivers a vibration. When it is digitised, this is measured at regular intervals.
88604.m: The higher the sampling rate, the more often a signal is measured per second.

88605.q: In which unit is the sampling rate given?
88605.e: Hertz means “per second”. 1000 hertz are 1000 measurements per second.
88605.m: The unit hertz means once per second.

88606.q: Why does music need a higher sampling rate than speech on the telephone?
88606.e: The higher a note, the faster it vibrates. To capture fast vibrations correctly, you have to measure more often, namely more than twice as often as the highest frequency.
88606.m: You have to measure more than twice as often as the highest frequency that occurs.

88607.q: Why does a voice on the telephone often sound duller than music from a CD?
a: The telephone measures the sound fewer times per second
The voice is lower than music
88607.e: Classic digital telephony measures only 8000 times per second, the CD 44,100 times. That is why the high notes are missing on the telephone.
88607.m: Telephone calls are transmitted with a low sampling rate.

88608.q: What happens to the file size if you double the sampling rate?
a: It becomes ten times as big
88608.e: Twice as many measurements per second means twice as much data. Without compression the file becomes about twice as big.
88608.m: More measurements per second need more storage space.

88609.q: Which component measures an analogue signal at regular intervals and turns it into numbers?
88609.e: The analogue-to-digital converter samples the signal and converts each measurement into a number.
88609.m: An analogue-to-digital converter turns vibrations into numbers.

88610.q: What happens if you measure a sound too few times per second?
88610.e: If the sampling rate is too low, high notes are wrongly recorded as lower notes or are lost. Experts call this error aliasing.
88610.m: Measuring too rarely creates false sounds.

88611.q: Which sampling rate records a sound most accurately?
88611.e: The higher the sampling rate, the more often the sound is measured per second and the more accurately it is recorded. For video sound 48 kHz is usual, for studio recordings also 96 kHz.
88611.m: Sound for videos is usually recorded at forty-eight kilohertz.

88612.q: What kind of compression does MP3 use?
88612.e: When converting to MP3, data is lost. The original cannot be restored exactly.
88612.m: MP3 makes music files smaller by removing data.

88613.q: Why did MP3 become so popular in the 1990s?
a: Because music files became much smaller
Because you no longer needed headphones
88613.e: With MP3, a song needed only a fraction of the storage. This made it easy to store music and send it over the internet.
88613.m: MP3 made music files small and easy to share.

88614.q: Which parts of the music does MP3 deliberately leave out when compressing?
a: Sounds that the ear can hardly hear
88614.e: MP3 uses psychoacoustics: quiet sounds next to loud ones are masked by the ear and can be dropped.
88614.m: MP3 mainly removes sounds that you can hardly hear anyway.

88615.q: An MP3 file is about eleven times smaller than the same song on CD. The song on CD needs 33 MB. Roughly how big is the MP3 file?
88615.m: An MP3 file is often only about an eleventh of the size of CD sound.

88616.q: Which MP3 bit rate gives the biggest file for the same length?
88616.e: The bit rate tells you how much data is stored per second. The higher it is, the bigger the file.
88616.m: A higher bit rate means better quality and bigger files.

88617.q: Roughly how big is a 3-minute MP3 file at 128 kbit/s?
88617.e: 180 seconds · 128 kbit = 23,040 kbit. Divided by 8 that gives 2880 kB, so about 2.9 MB.
88617.m: The file size comes from bit rate times duration.

88618.q: How does a music app know what an MP3 song is called and who sings it?
a: The details are stored in the file
The app guesses it from the melody
88618.e: An MP3 file has an area for extra information such as title, album and artist. This area is called the ID3 tag.
88618.m: MP3 files also store the title and artist.

a: A file format for music and sound
88619.e: MP3 is a format in which music and other sounds are stored in a space-saving way. Such files end in .mp3.
88619.m: MP3 is a format for music files.

88620.q: Which pictures is the JPEG format especially suited to?
88620.e: JPEG was developed for photos with many soft colour gradients. There the losses are hardly noticeable.
88620.m: JPEG is the typical format for photos.

88621.q: What does it mean that JPEG compresses a picture with loss?
a: Some picture details are lost when saving
The picture turns black and white
88621.e: JPEG leaves out details that you can hardly see. This makes the file much smaller, but the original can no longer be restored exactly.
88621.m: JPEG saves space by leaving out small picture details.

88622.q: What do you sometimes see in a heavily compressed JPEG picture?
a: More detail than in the original
88622.e: With heavy compression, JPEG leaves out many details. Then you can often see small squares and blurred edges.

88623.q: What happens if you edit a JPEG picture and save it again over and over?
a: The quality gets a little worse each time
The quality gets better each time
88623.e: Every time you save, it is compressed with loss again. The errors add up.
88623.m: A JPEG loses a little quality every time it is saved again.

88624.q: Which file extension do JPEG pictures often have?
88624.e: JPEG files usually end in .jpg or .jpeg.
88624.m: You can recognise a JPEG picture by the extension jpg.

88625.q: What does a low quality setting do when saving as JPEG?
a: A smaller file with more picture errors
A bigger file with fewer errors
88625.e: At low quality, more details are left out. The file gets smaller, but you can see more glitches.
88625.m: With JPEG you can weigh up a small file against good quality.

88626.q: Which pictures is JPEG rather poorly suited to?
a: Screenshots with text and sharp edges
88626.e: With JPEG, ugly glitches appear at sharp edges. For text and graphics, lossless formats are better.
88626.m: Text and sharp edges often look messy with JPEG.

88627.q: Why is JPEG so popular for photos on the internet?
a: The files are small and photos still look good
It can only store black and white
It plays music with the picture
88627.e: Small files load quickly and need little storage. With photos, the details left out are hardly noticeable.
88627.m: JPEG makes photo files small with good quality.

88628.q: Which animal eats fallen leaves in the forest floor and turns them into soil?
88628.e: Earthworms pull leaves into their tunnels and eat them. Their droppings are very good, loose soil.
88628.m: Earthworms turn leaves into good soil.

88629.q: What grows invisibly as a fine network in the forest floor?
88629.e: A fungus is mainly made of fine threads in the ground. What we see and call a mushroom is only its fruiting body.
88629.m: Most of a fungus lives hidden in the ground.

88630.q: What do trees get from the fungi on their roots?
88630.e: Many fungi grow closely around tree roots. They give the tree water and nutrients and get sugar in return.
88630.m: Fungi and trees help each other in the ground.

88631.q: What does the forest floor do with the rainwater that seeps through it?
88631.e: The forest floor works like a filter. That is why water from forest springs is usually very clean.
88631.m: Forest soil filters water and makes it clean.

88632.q: Which forest animal digs large burrows in the ground and likes eating earthworms?
88632.e: The badger digs large burrows with many tunnels using its strong claws. Earthworms are one of its favourite foods.
88632.m: The badger is a good digger in the forest floor.

88633.q: How does the forest floor behave in heavy rain?
a: It soaks up water like a sponge
88633.e: Loose forest soil stores lots of water. In this way the forest helps to prevent floods.
88633.m: Forest soil stores water like a sponge.

88634.q: Where in the forest floor do most small living things live?
88634.e: The top layer of soil has lots of food and air. Countless tiny animals, fungi and bacteria live there.
88634.m: The top of the forest floor is teeming with life.

88635.q: Which small animal with very many legs lives in the forest floor?
88635.e: Millipedes live hidden in damp soil and under stones. They eat dead plant parts.
88635.m: Millipedes help break down plant remains.

88636.q: Which plants make up the herb layer in the forest?
88636.e: The herb layer is just above the ground. Grasses, flowers, herbs and ferns grow there.
88636.m: Grasses, herbs and ferns grow in the herb layer.

88637.q: Which white spring flower often covers the ground in beech woods?
88637.e: The wood anemone flowers in March and April. It often forms a white carpet in deciduous woods.
88637.m: The wood anemone flowers early in deciduous woods.

88638.q: Why do many woodland flowers bloom as early as spring?
a: Lots of light reaches the ground then
All the forest animals are asleep then
88638.e: In spring the deciduous trees have no leaves yet. So lots of sunlight reaches the forest floor.
88638.m: Early flowers use the light before the trees have leaves.

88639.q: Which small woodland flower with violet petals smells nice in spring?
88639.e: Violets have heart-shaped leaves and like to grow in open deciduous woods. Some kinds smell sweet.

88640.q: Which woodland plant has no flowers but large feathery leaves?
88640.e: Ferns make no flowers and no seeds. They reproduce with tiny spores.

88641.q: Which woodland plant with clover-like leaves tastes sour?
88641.e: Wood sorrel has three heart-shaped little leaves. It contains acid, which is why it tastes sour.

88642.q: Which white woodland flower with little bells is poisonous?
88642.e: Lily of the valley flowers in May and has a strong scent. All parts of the plant are poisonous.
88642.m: Lilies of the valley are pretty but poisonous.

88643.q: Which blue berries grow on low little shrubs on the forest floor?
88643.e: Bilberries grow on small dwarf shrubs, often in coniferous forests. They turn your tongue and fingers blue.

88644.q: Which soft green cushions lie right at the bottom on the forest floor?
88644.e: Below the herb layer is the moss layer. Mosses store lots of water.
88644.m: Mosses form the lowest layer in the forest.

88645.q: Which woodland plant stings your skin when you touch it?
88645.e: The stinging nettle has fine stinging hairs. When you touch them, they break off and release a stinging liquid.
88645.m: The stinging nettle has stinging hairs.

88646.q: How tall do shrubs in the forest usually grow?
88646.e: Shrubs are bigger than herbs but smaller than trees. They usually grow about 1 to 5 metres tall.

88647.e: The hazel bush forms hazelnuts in autumn. Its catkins already flower in February.
88647.m: Hazelnuts grow on the hazel bush.

88648.q: Which prickly shrub bears sweet black berries?
88648.e: Brambles have prickly runners. Their berries, called blackberries, are red at first and black when ripe.

88649.q: Which shrub's white flowers are used to make cordial?
88649.e: The black elder has large, flat clusters of flowers. In Switzerland people like to make elderflower cordial from them.
88649.m: Elderflowers are used to make cordial.

88650.q: What do birds find in the shrub layer?
88650.e: Nests are well hidden in thick shrubs. The berries are important food in autumn.
88650.m: Shrubs give birds shelter and food.

88651.q: What else grows in the shrub layer besides shrubs?
88651.e: Young trees are still small, so they belong to the shrub layer. Later they grow up into the tree layer.
88651.m: Young trees grow up through the shrub layer.

88652.q: What are the red fruits of the dog rose called?
88652.e: The dog rose is a wild rose found at the edges of woods and in hedges. Its red fruits are called rosehips.
88652.m: Rosehips are the fruits of the wild rose.

88653.q: Which forest animal likes to eat the buds of shrubs and young trees?
88653.e: Roe deer like to nibble buds and young shoots. That is why young trees are sometimes protected with wire mesh.
88653.m: Roe deer like to eat young buds.

88654.q: Why do many birds build their nest high up in the treetop?
a: They are safe from enemies there
88654.e: Cats, foxes and martens find it hard to reach high up in the treetop. So eggs and chicks are safer there.
88654.m: Bird nests are well protected in the treetop.

88655.q: What do the leaves in the treetop do with sunlight?
a: They store it for the night
88655.e: With light, water and air, leaves make sugar. As they do this, they give off oxygen.
88655.m: Leaves use sunlight to make food for the tree.

88656.q: What do we call the closed roof made by many treetops?
88656.e: When the treetops touch, they form a roof over the forest. It is shady underneath.
88656.m: Many treetops together form the canopy.

88657.q: Which tree has leaves that look like a hand with fingers?
88657.e: Maple leaves usually have five pointed lobes. The leaf is also on the flag of Canada.
88657.m: Maple leaves look like a hand.

88658.q: Why is it cooler in the forest on hot summer days?
a: There is always a strong wind in the forest
The forest floor is made of stone
The bark of the trees is cold
88658.e: The treetops keep out lots of sun. The leaves also give off water, and this cools the air.
88658.m: Under the treetops it is pleasantly cool in summer.

88659.q: What is the highest layer in the forest called?
88659.e: The tree layer with the crowns of the big trees is right at the top. It gets the most light.
88659.m: The tree layer is the top layer in the forest.

88660.q: Which plant grows as a green ball high up in treetops?
88660.e: Mistletoe grows on the branches of trees. With its roots it taps into the tree and takes water from it.
88660.m: Mistletoe grows as a ball on trees.

88661.q: Which trees keep a green crown even in winter?
88661.e: Spruces, firs and pines keep their needles for several years. That is why they stay green in winter.
88661.m: Most conifers stay green in winter.

88662.e: Deadwood means dead trees, stumps and branches that lie or stand in the forest. It slowly breaks down over many years.
88662.m: Deadwood is dead wood that stays in the forest.

88663.q: Which large beetle spends its larval stage in rotten oak wood?
88663.e: The larva of the stag beetle lives in dead wood for several years. Only then does it turn into a beetle.
88663.m: The stag beetle needs dead wood for its larvae.

88664.q: Which living things break down deadwood especially strongly?
88664.e: Fungi grow into the wood with fine threads and make it soft. In this way the wood slowly turns into soil.
88664.m: Fungi help break down dead wood.

88665.q: Why do foresters sometimes leave dead trees standing in the forest?
a: They are a habitat for animals
88665.e: Beetles, fungi, birds and bats live in dead trees. That is why some deadwood is good for nature.
88665.m: Deadwood is a home for many animals.

88666.q: What is the part of a felled tree that stays in the ground called?
88666.e: After felling, the stump with its roots stays in the ground. Over time it rots and fungi and beetles move in.
88666.m: A tree stump slowly turns into soil.

88667.q: Which animal likes to spend the winter in a pile of branches and leaves?
88667.e: Piles of branches are warm and well hidden. Hedgehogs hibernate in them.
88667.m: Piles of branches are good winter homes for hedgehogs.

88668.q: What do lots of small bore holes in a dead tree trunk often show?
88668.e: Many beetles and their larvae bore tunnels into the wood. The little holes are often their exits.
88668.m: Small holes in wood often come from beetles.

88669.q: Who finds lots of food in the rotten wood of dead trees?
88669.e: Many beetle larvae live in rotten wood. Woodpeckers peck them out with their beaks.
88669.m: Woodpeckers find lots of larvae in deadwood.

a: An open space in the forest
88670.e: In a clearing there are no trees or hardly any. That is why lots of light reaches the ground there.
88670.m: A clearing is a bright spot in the forest.

88671.q: Why do especially many flowers grow in clearings?
88671.e: Without dense treetops, plants get lots of light there. Flowers and grasses benefit from this.
88671.m: Lots grows in clearings because it is bright.

88672.q: Which insects fly from flower to flower in sunny clearings?
88672.e: Butterflies love warm, sunny places with flowers. There they drink nectar.

88673.q: How can a clearing form in the forest?
88673.e: Strong storms can blow down lots of trees. Cutting down trees also creates open spaces.

88674.q: Which red berries often grow in bright clearings in the forest?
88674.e: Raspberries need lots of light. That is why they like to grow where there are no trees.
88674.m: Raspberries like bright spots in the forest.

88675.q: What happens to a clearing if it is left alone?
88675.e: First herbs grow, then shrubs and young trees. After many years there is forest there again.
88675.m: Over time a clearing turns back into forest.

88676.q: Which animals like to graze in forest clearings at dusk?
88676.e: Roe deer come out of the forest in the evening or early morning. In clearings they find grasses and herbs.
88676.m: Roe deer like to feed in clearings.

88677.q: Which animal likes to sunbathe on warm stones in a clearing?
88677.e: Lizards need the warmth of the sun to become active. In clearings they find sunny spots.
88677.m: Lizards warm up in the sun.

88678.q: What is the edge of a forest?
a: Where the forest meets the meadow
88678.e: At the edge of the forest the trees stop and meadows or fields begin. Two habitats mix there.
88678.m: At the forest edge, forest and meadow meet.

88679.q: Why do especially many kinds of animals live at the edge of the forest?
88679.e: At the forest edge animals find food from both forest and meadow. Shrubs also offer hiding places.
88679.m: There are many different animals at the forest edge.

88680.q: How is a good forest edge built up?
88680.e: A good forest edge starts with herbs, then come shrubs and finally tall trees. This creates many habitats.
88680.m: A good forest edge rises in steps.

88681.q: Which thorny shrub with blue fruits often grows at the edge of the forest?
88681.e: The blackthorn is also called sloe. It flowers white in spring and has blue, sour fruits called sloes.
88681.m: The blackthorn has thorns and blue fruits.

88682.q: Which bird of prey often sits at the edge of the forest and hunts mice?
88682.e: The common buzzard likes to sit on branches or posts at the forest edge. From there it watches for mice in the meadow.
88682.m: The buzzard hunts mice in meadows.

88683.q: What grows right on the outside of the forest edge, even before the shrubs?
88683.e: Right on the outside of the forest edge grow grasses and flowers. Behind them come shrubs and then the tall trees.
88683.m: Grasses and flowers grow right on the outside of the forest edge.

88684.q: How does a dense forest edge help the forest in a storm?
88684.e: Shrubs and low branches at the forest edge slow down the wind. So fewer trees are blown over.
88684.m: A dense forest edge protects the forest from wind.

88685.q: On which side is a forest edge usually warmest?
88685.e: In Switzerland the south side gets the most sun. Many warmth-loving animals and plants live there.
88685.m: Forest edges on the south side are especially warm.

88686.q: Whose job is it to look after the forest?
88686.e: Foresters plan which trees are cut down and which are protected. They make sure the forest stays healthy.
88686.m: The forester looks after the forest.

88687.q: What does the forester do before trees are cut down?
88687.e: The forester chooses the trees and marks them with paint. This way the forest workers know which ones to fell.
88687.m: The forester marks the trees that will be cut down.

88688.q: In Switzerland, what is the job of people who fell trees and look after the forest called?
88688.e: Forestry workers do an apprenticeship. They fell trees and plant and care for the forest.
88688.m: Forestry workers work in the forest every day.

88689.q: Which forest usually copes better with storms and heat?
a: Forest of one kind of tree
88689.e: In a mixed forest different kinds of trees grow. If one kind suffers, the others stay standing.
88689.m: A mixed forest is stronger than a forest of only one kind of tree.

88690.q: What does a forestry worker wear for protection when felling trees?
88690.e: When felling, branches can fall down and the chainsaw is loud. That is why forestry workers wear a helmet, ear protection and cut-resistant trousers.
88690.m: Anyone who fells trees wears protective clothing.

88691.q: In Switzerland the forest is protected. What usually has to be done if a piece of forest still has to go?
a: Build a fence round the forest
88691.e: In Switzerland you cannot simply clear forest. Anyone who is allowed to clear it usually has to plant a replacement somewhere else.
88691.m: Swiss forests are protected by law.

88692.q: What does a protection forest in the mountains protect against?
88692.e: Trees on steep slopes hold back snow and stones. In this way they protect villages and roads.
88692.m: Protection forests protect people from avalanches and rockfalls.

88693.q: In Switzerland, are you allowed to walk in a forest that belongs to someone else?
a: Yes, the forest is open to everyone
88693.e: In Switzerland everyone may walk in the forest, even someone else's. But you must show respect for nature and animals.
88693.m: Swiss forests are open to everyone.

88694.q: What is wood from the forest used for?
88694.e: Wood is a renewable raw material. People build houses and furniture from it or use it for heating.
88694.m: Wood is used for building and heating.

88695.q: Which ants build the big mounds in the forest?
88695.e: Red wood ants build mounds that can be over a metre high. They live mainly in coniferous forests.
88695.m: Red wood ants build big anthills.

88696.q: What is the ant that lays the eggs in an anthill called?
88696.e: The queens lay the eggs from which the colony grows. The many workers look after the young and fetch food.
88696.m: The queen lays the eggs in an ant colony.

88697.q: Why must you not destroy an anthill in Switzerland?
88697.e: Red wood ants have been protected in Switzerland since 1966. Their nests must not be damaged.
88697.m: Wood ants are protected in Switzerland.

88698.q: Which acid do wood ants spray to defend themselves?
88698.e: Wood ants can spray formic acid. It stings and drives enemies away.
88698.m: Wood ants defend themselves with formic acid.

88699.q: Which sweet liquid do ants like to collect from aphids?
88699.e: Aphids give off a sugary liquid called honeydew. The ants drink it and protect the aphids in return.
88699.m: Ants drink the honeydew of aphids.

88700.q: Why are wood ants useful for the forest?
a: They eat lots of pest insects
They chase away all the birds
88700.e: An ant colony catches huge numbers of insects, including pests. That is why they are called the health police of the forest.
88700.m: Wood ants keep the forest healthy.

88701.q: Where do wood ants most like to build their mounds?
a: In the middle of a stream
88701.e: Ants need warmth for their young. That is why anthills are often at the edges of woods or in sunny places.
88701.m: Anthills like to be in the sun.

88702.q: How many ants can live in a big anthill?
88702.e: A big colony of red wood ants can have several hundred thousand ants. They all work together.
88702.m: Very many ants live in an anthill.

88703.q: Why does a woodpecker hammer against trees with its beak?
a: To look for food and make holes
88703.e: Woodpeckers search the wood for larvae and carve out nesting holes. To do this they peck with their strong beak.
88703.m: The woodpecker pecks wood for food and to make holes.

88704.q: What does the woodpecker use to get insects out of narrow holes?
88704.e: Woodpeckers have a very long tongue with barbs. With it they pull larvae out of their tunnels.
88704.m: The woodpecker has a very long tongue.

88705.q: Which woodpecker is the most common in Switzerland?
88705.e: The great spotted woodpecker is black, white and red. You find it in almost every forest and even in gardens.
88705.m: The great spotted woodpecker is the most common woodpecker in Switzerland.

88706.q: Which woodpecker is the biggest in Europe?
88706.e: The black woodpecker is almost as big as a crow. It is black and has a red cap.
88706.m: The black woodpecker is the biggest woodpecker in Europe.

88707.q: Which woodpecker often looks for food on the ground and likes eating ants?
88707.e: The green woodpecker has green feathers. It pokes about in meadows looking for ants.
88707.m: The green woodpecker loves eating ants.

88708.q: What does the woodpecker prop itself up with when climbing a trunk?
88708.e: The woodpecker has hard, stiff tail feathers. It presses them against the trunk like a prop.
88708.m: The woodpecker props itself up with its tail.

88709.q: Who often moves into old woodpecker holes?
88709.e: Woodpeckers like to make new holes every year. Other animals such as tits, owls or bats use the old ones.
88709.m: Old woodpecker holes are a home for many animals.

88710.q: Why does a woodpecker drum loudly on branches in spring?
88710.e: The drumming can be heard a long way off. With it the woodpecker tells other woodpeckers: this is where I live.
88710.m: Woodpeckers drum to show their territory.

88711.q: What is the round nest of a squirrel called?
88711.e: A drey is made of twigs and lined with moss inside. It sits high up in a treetop.
88711.m: The squirrel sleeps in a drey.

88712.q: What do squirrels do with nuts in autumn?
a: They hide them as a store
They throw them into the stream
They build a nest out of them
They give them to the birds
88712.e: Squirrels bury nuts and seeds in lots of places. In winter they look for these stores again.

a: No, it has a winter rest
No, it is as awake as in summer
Yes, it sleeps without a break until spring
88713.e: Squirrels sleep a lot in winter but keep waking up. Then they eat from their stores.
88713.m: Squirrels have a winter rest, not true hibernation.

88714.q: What happens to nuts that a squirrel forgets?
88714.e: Many hidden seeds are never found. In spring they sprout, and new trees grow.
88714.m: Squirrels plant new trees without meaning to.

88715.q: What does the squirrel especially like to eat?
88715.e: Squirrels mainly eat nuts, acorns and seeds from fir cones. Sometimes they also eat buds or mushrooms.

88716.q: Which predator hunts squirrels high up in the trees?
88716.e: The pine marten is a very skilful climber. It can chase squirrels right up into the treetops.
88716.m: The pine marten is an enemy of the squirrel.

88717.q: What colour is a squirrel's belly?
88717.e: The fur on its back is reddish brown to blackish brown. But the belly is always pale to white.

88718.e: In autumn the leaves fall onto the forest floor. Together with needles and twigs they form the leaf litter.
88718.m: Leaf litter is the layer of leaves on the forest floor.

88719.q: Which small grey animals with armour like to eat damp leaves?
88719.e: Woodlice live under leaves, stones and wood. They need moisture and eat dead plant parts.

88720.q: How does leaf litter help the soil in winter?
a: It keeps it warm and moist
88720.e: The layer of leaves works like a blanket. It protects the soil from frost and drying out.
88720.m: Leaf litter is like a blanket for the soil.

88721.q: Which bird often tosses leaves about while looking for food?
88721.e: Blackbirds turn over leaves with their beaks. Underneath they find worms and insects.
88721.m: Blackbirds look under leaves for worms.

88722.q: Why should leaves be left lying in the forest?
a: They give nutrients back to the soil
They hold the trees in place
88722.e: When leaves break down, the nutrients go back into the soil. The trees take them up again.
88722.m: Old leaves feed the forest soil.

88723.q: What does leaf litter turn into over time?
88723.e: Soil animals, fungi and bacteria break down the leaves. This creates dark, fertile soil.

88724.q: Why do leaves turn yellow and red in autumn?
a: The green chlorophyll is broken down
88724.e: In autumn the tree breaks down the green chlorophyll. Then other colours in the leaves become visible.
88724.m: In autumn the green disappears from the leaves.

88725.q: Which animals like to hide in damp leaf litter?
88725.e: Under the leaves it is damp and shady. Snails find shelter and food there.

88813.q: Which organ fills with air when you breathe in?
88813.e: When you breathe in, air flows into the lungs. There the body takes what it needs to live.
88813.m: When you breathe in, your lungs fill with air.

88814.q: Which muscle under the lungs helps most with breathing in?
88814.e: The diaphragm is a flat muscle under the lungs. When it tightens, space is made and air flows in.
88814.m: The diaphragm is our most important breathing muscle.

88815.q: Where in the body are the lungs?
88815.e: The lungs fill almost the whole chest. The ribs protect them on all sides.
88815.m: The lungs are in the chest.

88816.q: Why is the left lung slightly smaller than the right?
88816.e: The heart lies a little more on the left side of the chest. That is why the left lung is a bit smaller.
88816.m: The heart needs room next to the left lung.

88817.q: Where does the air you breathe in end up in the end?
a: In the air sacs of the lungs
88817.e: The air travels through finer and finer tubes into tiny air sacs. There the body takes in the oxygen.
88817.m: The air ends up in the tiny air sacs.

88818.q: Through which openings of the body can we breathe in?
88818.e: Air enters the body through the nose or the mouth. The ears and eyes are not connected to the lungs.
