91788.e: Moonlight is far too weak to burn your skin. You only get sunburn from the sun.

91789.q: Which side of the Moon do we always see from Earth?
91789.e: The Moon turns around itself exactly as fast as it goes round the Earth. That is why it always shows us the same side.
91789.m: We always see the same side of the Moon.

91891.q: Which atoms make up a molecule of carbon dioxide?
a: One carbon and two oxygen atoms
Two carbon and one oxygen atom
One carbon and four hydrogen atoms
One carbon and one oxygen atom
91891.e: The formula CO2 shows one carbon atom (C) and two oxygen atoms (O). The molecule is straight, but it can vibrate and absorb heat radiation as it does so.
91891.m: A carbon dioxide molecule consists of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.

91892.q: What kind of radiation do greenhouse gases hold back in the atmosphere?
91892.e: The Earth's surface gives off heat as infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb this radiation and send part of it back to Earth.
91892.m: Greenhouse gases trap the Earth's heat radiation.

91893.q: What is the warming effect of the air around the Earth compared to?
91893.e: Like the glass of a greenhouse, the atmosphere holds back part of the heat. That is where the name greenhouse effect comes from.
91893.m: The atmosphere warms the Earth in a similar way to a greenhouse.

91894.q: What is the greenhouse gas nitrous oxide (N2O) commonly called?
91894.e: Nitrous oxide is called laughing gas because of its earlier use as an anaesthetic. It is produced mainly by nitrogen fertiliser in farming.
91894.m: Laughing gas is a strong greenhouse gas from farming.

91895.q: Since when have scientists known that more carbon dioxide can warm the Earth?
91895.e: As early as 1896, the Swede Svante Arrhenius calculated that more carbon dioxide makes the Earth warmer. So the idea is more than 100 years old.
91895.m: The warming effect of CO2 has been known for more than 100 years.

91897.q: Which natural greenhouse gas is the most common in the air?
91897.e: Water vapour is the most common greenhouse gas. How much of it is in the air depends mainly on the temperature.
91897.m: Water vapour is the most common natural greenhouse gas.

91898.q: Which two main components of air are not greenhouse gases?
91898.e: Nitrogen and oxygen together make up about 99 per cent of dry air. Their molecules, made of two identical atoms, hardly absorb any heat radiation.
91898.m: The main gases in air, nitrogen and oxygen, do not act as greenhouse gases.

91899.q: What does the Keeling Curve show?
a: The CO2 content of the air
The thickness of the ozone layer
91899.e: The Keeling Curve shows the measured concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. It has risen steadily since measurements began.
91899.m: The Keeling Curve shows the rise of carbon dioxide in the air.

91900.q: Why is the CO2 content for the Keeling Curve measured on a high mountain far away from cities?
a: Because the air there is hardly affected by nearby exhaust fumes
Because lots of plants grow there
Because the wind never blows there
91900.e: In cities, cars and heating systems would distort the measurement. On a remote mountain you measure the well-mixed air of the whole Earth.
91900.m: Accurate CO2 measurements need clean air far away from cities.

91901.q: Overall, how has the Keeling Curve developed since measurements began?
a: It rises and falls by the same amount
91901.e: Despite a small up and down every year, the curve keeps going up. So the CO2 content of the air is constantly increasing.
91901.m: The Keeling Curve shows a steady rise in CO2.

91902.q: Where does most of the extra CO2 shown by the Keeling Curve come from?
a: From burning coal, oil and gas
91902.e: Since industrialisation, people have burned huge amounts of coal, oil and gas. This produces CO2, which builds up in the air.
91902.m: The rise in CO2 comes mainly from coal, oil and gas.

91903.q: Why does the Keeling Curve show a small up and down every year?
a: Plants take in CO2 in summer
The instruments are calibrated every year
The sun shines more strongly in winter
91903.e: There are many more land plants in the Northern Hemisphere. When they grow in summer they take in carbon dioxide; in autumn and winter some is released again as leaves decompose.
91903.m: The yearly up and down of the Keeling Curve is the breathing of plants.

91904.q: Why is the Keeling Curve so important for climate research?
a: For decades it has shown without a break how much CO2 is in the air
It measures the strength of earthquakes
It shows the temperature of seawater
91904.e: The series of measurements has run without a break since 1958. It was one of the first clear pieces of evidence that the CO2 content of the air is rising.
91904.m: The Keeling Curve is one of the most important records in climate research.

91905.q: How has the CO2 content of the air changed since the Keeling Curve began?
a: It has risen by about a third
91905.e: When measurements began, the value was about 315 ppm; today it is over 420 ppm. That is about a third more.
91905.m: The CO2 content of the air has risen by about a third since 1958.

91906.q: Roughly what value did the CO2 content of the air reach on Mauna Loa as the annual average for 2024?
91906.e: The annual average for 2024 on Mauna Loa was just under 425 ppm (as of 2024). That is the highest value for hundreds of thousands of years.
91906.m: The CO2 content of the air is now over 420 ppm.

91907.q: What does the unit ppm, used for the Keeling Curve, stand for?
91907.e: The abbreviation ppm stands for “parts per million”. 420 ppm means that out of a million particles of air, 420 are carbon dioxide.
91907.m: The unit ppm means parts per million.

91908.q: What is the chemical formula of methane?
91908.e: A methane molecule consists of one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. It is the simplest hydrocarbon.

91909.q: Which animals release a particularly large amount of methane during digestion?
91909.e: Cattle are ruminants. In their rumen, microorganisms break down grass and produce methane, which the animals mainly burp out.
91909.m: Ruminants such as cattle are a big source of methane.

91910.q: Growing which food crop produces a particularly large amount of methane?
91910.e: Rice fields are often under water. In the oxygen-poor mud, bacteria break down plant remains and produce methane.
91910.m: Flooded rice fields are an important source of methane.

91911.q: How strongly does methane warm compared to the same amount of CO2?
91911.e: Per kilogram, methane holds back much more heat than carbon dioxide. Calculated over 100 years, it is almost 30 times as effective.
91911.m: Per kilogram, methane is a much stronger greenhouse gas than CO2.

91912.q: Why does it help the climate quickly when less methane is emitted?
a: Methane breaks down in the air after a few years
Methane stays in the air for ever
Methane sinks to the ground immediately
91912.e: In the air, methane is slowly broken down into carbon dioxide and water, on average in about 12 years. That is why cutting methane emissions works relatively quickly.
91912.m: Methane breaks down in the air after about twelve years.

91913.q: Which fossil fuel consists mainly of methane?
91913.e: Natural gas usually consists of 80 to 99 per cent methane. If it escapes unburnt from pipes or boreholes, it acts as a strong greenhouse gas.

91914.q: What other name is used for methane that forms in wet bogs?
91914.e: In swamps and bogs, bacteria break down plant remains without oxygen. Methane rises in bubbles, which is why it is also called marsh gas.
91914.m: Methane from swamps is also called marsh gas.

91915.q: Why can you smell natural gas when it escapes from a pipe?
a: A smelly substance is added to it
It turns into sulphur in the air
The pipes give off the smell
91915.e: Pure methane has no smell. So that a leak is noticed at once, a strong-smelling substance is added to natural gas.
91915.m: For safety, a smelly substance is added to natural gas.

91916.q: Which of these fuels is not a fossil fuel?
91916.e: Fossil fuels formed millions of years ago from dead living things. Wood, on the other hand, keeps growing back and counts as a renewable fuel.
91916.m: Wood is a renewable fuel, not a fossil fuel.

91917.q: What did crude oil and natural gas mainly form from?
91917.e: Tiny sea creatures sank to the seabed after they died. Under pressure and heat, their remains turned into oil and natural gas over millions of years.
91917.m: Oil formed from plankton deposited millions of years ago.

91918.q: Which living things did hard coal mainly form from?
91918.e: Giant ferns, horsetails and club moss trees grew in swamp forests. Their remains were covered over and, without air, turned via peat and lignite into hard coal.
91918.m: Coal is transformed wood from ancient swamp forests.

91919.q: Which geological period is named after coal?
91919.e: The name Carboniferous comes from the Latin word “carbo” for coal. During this period, about 359 to 299 million years ago, many large coal deposits formed.
91919.m: The Carboniferous is the age of the coal forests.

91920.q: Why does burning fossil fuels permanently increase the CO2 content of the air?
a: Carbon stored for a long time is released
The CO2 comes from the air in the engine
91920.e: The carbon in coal, oil and natural gas was locked in the ground for millions of years. When it is burned, it enters today's cycle as extra carbon dioxide.
91920.m: Fossil fuels bring ancient carbon back into the atmosphere.

91921.q: Which fuel releases the most CO2 for the amount of energy produced?
91921.e: Lignite contains a lot of water and, compared to its energy, a lot of carbon. Natural gas causes only about half as much carbon dioxide for the same energy.
91921.m: Lignite is the most climate-damaging fossil fuel.

91922.q: What happens in an oil refinery?
a: Crude oil is made into petrol, diesel and heating oil
Oil is pumped out of the ground
Oil is purified into drinking water
91922.e: In a refinery, crude oil is heated and separated into different components. In Switzerland, only the refinery at Cressier in the canton of Neuchâtel is still operating.
91922.m: A refinery turns crude oil into petrol, diesel and heating oil.

91923.q: Which country produced the most oil in 2023?
91923.e: Thanks to production from shale rock, the USA has been the world's largest oil producer since 2018 (as of 2023). Saudi Arabia and Russia come next.
91923.m: The USA is currently the world's largest oil producer.

91924.q: In which year was the Paris Agreement adopted?
91924.e: In December 2015, almost all countries in the world agreed on a new climate agreement in Paris. It is the first in which all countries commit to protecting the climate.
91924.m: The Paris climate agreement dates from 2015.

91925.q: To what value does the Paris Agreement aim to limit global warming if possible?
91925.e: Warming should stay well below 2 °C. Countries also want to make efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C.
91925.m: The Paris goal is warming of only 1.5 degrees if possible.

91926.q: Compared to which time is warming measured in the Paris Agreement?
91926.e: The comparison is the climate before industrialisation, usually the period 1850 to 1900. Since then, the Earth has already warmed by well over 1 °C.
91926.m: The climate goals refer to the temperature before industrialisation.

91927.q: What is the annual UN climate conference, where the Paris Agreement was also adopted, called?
91927.e: COP stands for “Conference of the Parties”. Every year, the countries that adopted the climate agreement in Paris in 2015 meet there.
91927.m: At the UN climate conference COP, countries negotiate on climate protection.

91928.q: What must the countries in the Paris Agreement submit every five years?
a: A list of their coal power stations
A contribution to the UN army
91928.e: Each country decides for itself how much it wants to cut its emissions. These national contributions are supposed to be renewed and tightened every five years.
91928.m: In the Paris Agreement, each country sets its own climate targets and raises them regularly.

91929.q: Which country left the Paris Agreement under President Donald Trump?
91929.e: Under Donald Trump, the USA announced its withdrawal, which took effect in 2020. President Joe Biden rejoined in 2021, and in 2025 Trump announced withdrawal again, which took effect at the beginning of 2026.
91929.m: The USA has joined and left the Paris Agreement more than once.

91930.q: Which older climate agreement from 1997 came before the Paris Agreement?
91930.e: In Kyoto, Japan, in 1997, mainly industrialised countries agreed binding targets to cut their emissions. The Paris Agreement, by contrast, includes all countries.
91930.m: The Kyoto Protocol of 1997 was the forerunner of the Paris Agreement.

91931.q: By how much does Switzerland want to cut its greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared to 1990?
91931.e: Under the Paris Agreement, Switzerland has promised to halve its emissions by 2030. Part of this may be achieved through climate protection projects abroad.
91931.m: Switzerland wants to halve its emissions by 2030 compared to 1990.

91932.q: What topic does the IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) deal with?
91932.e: Since 1988, the IPCC has gathered knowledge about climate change, its causes and its effects.
91932.m: The IPCC deals with climate change.

91933.q: Which big international organisation does the IPCC belong to?
91933.e: The IPCC was founded by two United Nations organisations. Almost all countries in the world take part.
91933.m: The IPCC belongs to the United Nations.

91934.q: In which Swiss city is the secretariat of the IPCC based?
91934.e: The IPCC secretariat is in Geneva at the headquarters of the World Meteorological Organization. Geneva is home to many international organisations.
91934.m: The IPCC has its secretariat in Geneva.

91935.q: What is the main task of the IPCC?
a: To summarise the state of climate research
To run its own weather stations
To pass climate laws for all countries
To fine people who harm the environment
91935.e: The IPCC does not do research itself. Thousands of experts volunteer to assess published research and summarise it in assessment reports for politicians.
91935.m: The IPCC summarises climate research for politicians.

91936.q: Which prize did the IPCC receive in 2007?
91936.e: The IPCC shared the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize with former US Vice President Al Gore. They were honoured for their work spreading knowledge about climate change.
91936.m: The IPCC was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2007.

91937.q: What does the 2023 IPCC report confirm?
a: The climate is not changing at all
Only the sun is causing the warming
91937.e: The report summarises the knowledge from thousands of studies. It states that humans are clearly causing the warming.
91937.m: According to the IPCC, humans are causing global warming.

91938.q: What does it mean when a country is climate-neutral?
a: It no longer emits any greenhouse gases on balance
It has the same weather every year
It uses no energy at all
It is not affected by climate change
91938.e: Climate-neutral means that no more greenhouse gases are emitted than are removed from the air again. So the balance is net zero.
91938.m: Climate neutrality means a greenhouse gas balance of net zero.

91939.q: By which year does Switzerland want to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions?
91939.e: In 2019, the Federal Council decided on the goal of net zero by 2050. This goal is now written into the Climate Act.
91939.m: Switzerland wants to be climate-neutral by 2050.

91940.q: Who confirmed the net zero by 2050 goal at the ballot box in Switzerland in June 2023?
91940.e: In Switzerland, the people can vote on laws. About 59 per cent said yes to the Climate and Innovation Act with the goal of net zero by 2050.
91940.m: Voters confirmed the net zero goal in 2023.

91941.q: What is meant by CO2 offsetting?
a: Making up for emissions through climate projects elsewhere
91941.e: Anyone who offsets emissions pays for projects that save or capture the same amount of greenhouse gases elsewhere. But this does not make their own emissions smaller.
91941.m: With offsetting, emissions are balanced out by climate protection somewhere else.

91942.q: What is the technology called that uses fans and filters to take carbon dioxide directly from the surrounding air?
91942.e: In direct air capture, fans draw air through a filter that captures carbon dioxide. An early plant of this kind was developed in Switzerland.
91942.m: Direct air capture can filter carbon dioxide out of the air.

91943.q: Which emissions are considered especially hard to avoid and must be balanced out by removing CO2 to reach net zero?
91943.e: When limestone is burned to make cement, chemically bound CO2 is released, no matter how it is heated. To reach net zero, such remaining emissions have to be balanced out with negative emissions.
91943.m: Remaining emissions that are hard to avoid must be balanced out for net zero.

91944.q: What is done when CO2 is stored underground?
a: CO2 is captured and stored deep in the rock
Old caves are filled with rubbish
Oil is pumped to the surface
Electricity is stored in big batteries
91944.e: At factories such as cement works, the CO2 is filtered out of the exhaust gases. It is then pressed deep underground so that it does not get into the air.
91944.m: CO2 can be captured and stored underground.

91945.q: Which heating system uses heat from the air, ground or water and is increasingly replacing oil heating in Switzerland?
91945.e: A heat pump uses a little electricity to take heat from the surroundings and raise it to heating temperature. With electricity from renewable sources, you can heat almost without CO2 emissions.
91945.m: Heat pumps help to heat buildings in a climate-friendly way.

91946.q: What does the carbon footprint show?
91946.e: The carbon footprint adds up all the greenhouse gases caused by a person, a product or a company. It includes things like heating, transport, food and shopping.
91946.m: The carbon footprint measures the climate impact of what we do.

91947.q: In which unit is a person's carbon footprint usually given?
a: Tonnes of CO2 equivalent per year
91947.e: All greenhouse gases are converted into their effect as carbon dioxide. For a person, the result is usually given in tonnes per year.
91947.m: A personal footprint is measured in tonnes of CO2 equivalent per year.

91948.q: Which means of transport causes the smallest carbon footprint per passenger kilometre?
91948.e: Cycling burns no fuel. Only making the bike and the extra food you eat count.
91948.m: Cycling is one of the most climate-friendly ways to get around.

91949.q: Which food usually has the biggest carbon footprint per kilogram?
91949.e: Cattle need a lot of feed and land and give off methane. That is why a kilogram of beef causes many times the emissions of plant foods.
91949.m: Beef is one of the most climate-damaging foods.

91950.q: How can a family make its carbon footprint smaller?
a: Go on holiday by train instead of by plane
91950.e: Flying causes a lot of CO2 per trip. Travelling by train saves a large part of it.
91950.m: Train instead of plane makes the carbon footprint smaller.

91951.q: What is the energy needed to make, transport and dispose of a product called?
91951.e: Embodied energy is hidden in every product, such as a mobile phone or a house. It often makes up a large part of the carbon footprint.
91951.m: Every product contains embodied energy from the way it was made.

91952.q: Why do strawberries often have a bigger carbon footprint in winter than in summer?
a: They are flown in or grown with heating
They contain more sugar in winter
They don't need to be cooled in winter
91952.e: In winter, no strawberries grow outdoors in Switzerland. They then often come by plane or from heated greenhouses, which uses a lot of energy.
91952.m: Seasonal and local food usually has a smaller footprint.

91953.q: What does stating something in CO2 equivalents mean?
a: Other gases are converted into their CO2 effect
The CO2 is converted into litres
The amount is divided by two
91953.e: Methane and laughing gas warm more strongly than carbon dioxide. So that everything can be added up, their amount is converted into the equivalent amount of CO2.
91953.m: CO2 equivalents make different greenhouse gases comparable.

91954.q: Why does sea level rise with warming even when no ice melts?
91954.e: Water takes up more space at higher temperatures. This thermal expansion of the ocean is one of the main causes of the rise, along with melting glaciers.
91954.m: Warmer seawater expands and makes sea level rise.

91955.q: Why does melting sea ice hardly make sea level rise?
a: Because it is already floating in the water
Because it is made of fresh water and sinks
Because it only melts in winter
91955.e: Floating ice already displaces as much water as it weighs. When it melts, the water level hardly changes, which is very different from ice on land.
91955.m: Only melting land ice makes sea level rise noticeably.

91956.q: Which island nation in the Pacific is particularly threatened by rising sea levels?
91956.e: Tuvalu consists of flat atolls that are mostly only a few metres above the sea. Even a small rise leads to flooding and salty groundwater there.
91956.m: Low-lying island nations like Tuvalu face a threat to their very existence from rising sea levels.

91957.q: Which measuring device has long been used to measure the water level on coasts?
91957.e: A tide gauge continuously measures the height of the water level at a fixed place. Since 1993, satellites have also measured sea level worldwide.
91957.m: Tide gauges and satellites measure the rise in sea level.

91958.q: By roughly how much does the average sea level rise each year today?
91958.e: According to the IPCC, the rise from 2006 to 2018 was about 3.7 millimetres per year. That is more than twice as fast as in the 20th century.
91958.m: Sea level is now rising by a few millimetres every year.

91959.q: Which European country lies about a quarter below sea level?
91959.e: Large parts of the Netherlands were reclaimed from the sea and lie lower than sea level. Dykes, dunes and storm surge barriers protect the country.
91959.m: The Netherlands protects itself from the sea with dykes.

91960.q: Where is the largest ice sheet on Earth?
91960.e: The Antarctic ice sheet covers almost the whole continent and is more than 4 kilometres thick in places. It is much bigger than the Greenland ice sheet.
91960.m: Antarctica has the largest ice sheet on Earth.

91961.q: What does the ice at the geographic North Pole lie on?
91961.e: There is no land at the North Pole, only sea. The ice there is floating sea ice that is only a few metres thick.
91961.m: The ice at the North Pole floats on the sea.

91962.q: In which month is the area of Arctic sea ice at its smallest each year?
91962.e: Sea ice melts all through the summer and reaches its smallest extent in September. This September area has shrunk a lot since 1979.
91962.m: Arctic sea ice reaches its smallest area in September.

91963.q: What is the reflectivity of a surface called, which is especially high for ice?
91963.e: Bright ice reflects a large part of the sunlight. When it melts, the dark sea absorbs more heat, which makes the warming even stronger.
91963.m: The high albedo of ice protects the Earth from too much heat from the sun.

91964.q: Where is most of the Earth's fresh water stored?
91964.e: The Antarctic ice sheet holds about 60 per cent of all the fresh water on Earth. Rivers, lakes and clouds contain much less.
91964.m: More than half of the Earth's fresh water is frozen in the ice of Antarctica.

91965.q: What can scientists learn from ice cores from Antarctica?
a: The climate and air of earlier times
91965.e: Tiny air bubbles thousands of years old are trapped in the ice. Scientists, including at the University of Bern, use them to measure earlier temperatures and gas levels.
91965.m: Ice cores are an archive of the climate of past millennia.

91966.q: Roughly how thick is the Greenland ice sheet at its thickest point?
91966.e: In the middle of Greenland the ice is more than 3000 metres thick. Its weight has even pushed the bedrock below sea level.
91966.m: The Greenland ice sheet is up to about three kilometres thick.

91967.q: Which animal hunts seals on the Arctic sea ice and therefore depends on the ice?
91967.e: Polar bears lie in wait on the ice by the breathing holes of seals. If the sea ice melts earlier, they have less time to hunt.
91967.m: The polar bear needs the sea ice to hunt.

91968.q: Over which area does the largest ozone hole form each year?
91968.e: The extreme cold over the South Pole encourages chemical reactions that destroy ozone. That is why ozone loss is strongest there.
91968.m: The ozone hole forms mainly over Antarctica.

91969.q: In which season of the Southern Hemisphere is the ozone hole at its biggest?
91969.e: When the sun returns after the polar night, its light starts the reactions that destroy ozone. That is why the ozone hole is biggest in September and October.
91969.m: The ozone hole is biggest in the southern spring.

91970.q: Which substances are the main cause of the ozone hole?
91970.e: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) used to be used in spray cans and fridges. High up, they release chlorine, which destroys ozone.

91971.q: Which agreement from 1987 gradually banned CFCs worldwide?
91971.e: In the Montreal Protocol, countries agreed to get rid of substances that damage the ozone layer. It is seen as one of the most successful environmental agreements.
91971.m: The Montreal Protocol protects the ozone layer.

91972.q: What does the ozone layer protect us from?
91972.e: The ozone layer absorbs a large part of the sun's ultraviolet radiation. Too much UV radiation can cause sunburn and skin cancer.
91972.m: The ozone layer filters out dangerous UV radiation.

91973.q: In which layer of the atmosphere is the ozone layer mainly found?
91973.e: Most ozone molecules are found at a height of about 15 to 35 kilometres. This layer lies above the weather layer and is called the stratosphere.
91973.m: The ozone layer is in the stratosphere.

91974.q: How was the ozone hole discovered in the 1980s?
a: Through measurements by scientists in Antarctica
Through photos taken by aeroplane passengers
Through a chance find in a desert
91974.e: Scientists of the British Antarctic Survey measured a sharp drop in ozone over Antarctica and reported it in 1985. The discovery quickly led to international action.
91974.m: The ozone hole was discovered through measurements in Antarctica.

91975.q: What have scientists in Arosa and Davos been measuring for almost 100 years?
a: The amount of ozone in the air
91975.e: Regular ozone measurements began in Arosa in 1926. Today MeteoSwiss continues the world's longest series of ozone measurements in Davos.
91975.m: The world's oldest series of ozone measurements began in Arosa.

91976.q: What has been happening to the ozone hole since CFCs were banned?
a: It is getting bigger every year
It has moved to the North Pole
91976.e: Thanks to the ban on CFCs, ozone loss is decreasing. Experts expect the ozone layer over Antarctica to recover by about 2066.
91976.m: The ozone layer is slowly recovering because CFCs were banned.

91977.q: What is a tipping point in the climate system?
a: A threshold with effects that are hard to reverse
The warmest day of a year
A measuring point on a mountain
The change from day to night
91977.e: If a tipping point is passed, part of the climate system changes suddenly. The change often cannot be undone, even if the temperature falls again.
91977.m: After a tipping point, a climate system often changes for good.

91978.q: What could get into the air if permafrost thaws over large areas?
91978.e: Huge amounts of plant remains are stored in the frozen ground. If it thaws, microorganisms break them down and release greenhouse gases, which makes the warming stronger.
91978.m: Thawing permafrost can release extra greenhouse gases.

91979.q: What could the Amazon rainforest turn into after passing a tipping point?
91979.e: Because of deforestation and drought, the rainforest could produce too little of its own rain. Parts of it could then become dry grassland.
91979.m: The Amazon rainforest is seen as a possible tipping element.

91980.q: Which ocean current is seen as a possible tipping element because meltwater could weaken it?
91980.e: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, which includes the Gulf Stream, carries warm water northwards. Lots of fresh water from Greenland could slow it down, which would greatly change the climate in Europe.
91980.m: A weaker Atlantic overturning circulation would have big effects on Europe.

91981.q: Which ecosystem dies off through so-called bleaching when seawater is too warm?
91981.e: When the water is too warm, corals expel their colourful algae and turn white. If the heat lasts, they die, and whole reefs can be lost.
91981.m: Warm-water corals are especially sensitive to warming.

91982.q: What is ground that stays frozen without a break for at least two years called?
91982.e: There is permafrost in Siberia, Canada and Alaska, but also high up in the Swiss Alps. If it thaws in the mountains, rockfalls can become more frequent.

91983.q: What is a self-reinforcing feedback in the climate system?
a: An effect strengthens its own cause
An effect cancels out its cause
A measuring error at weather stations
91983.e: For example, warming makes ice melt, and less ice leads to even more warming. Such reinforcing feedbacks can push a system past a tipping point.
91983.m: Reinforcing feedbacks can speed up climate change.

91984.q: What would the collapse of the West Antarctic ice sheet cause in the long term?
a: A sea level rise of several metres
A new ice age in Europe
More sea ice in the Arctic
91984.e: The West Antarctic ice sheet rests on bedrock below sea level and is therefore vulnerable to warm seawater. Its ice is enough for a rise of about three metres.
91984.m: The West Antarctic ice sheet is a threatened tipping element.

91985.q: Which gas from the air is put into crisp packets as a protective gas so that the crisps do not go rancid?
91985.e: Nitrogen hardly reacts with food. It pushes the oxygen out of the packet, which would otherwise spoil the fat in the crisps.
91985.m: Nitrogen protects packaged food from going off.

91986.q: What is liquid nitrogen used for, for example?
91986.e: Liquid nitrogen is extremely cold. So it is used for flash freezing and in medicine for freezing tissue.
91986.m: Liquid nitrogen is extremely cold and is used for freezing.

91987.q: Roughly how much of the air is carbon dioxide?
91987.e: Carbon dioxide is only a trace gas: out of 10,000 air particles, about 4 are CO2. Even so, it has a big effect on the climate.
91987.m: The air contains only traces of carbon dioxide.

91988.q: How is air classified in chemistry?
91988.e: The gases in the air are only mixed, not chemically bonded together. So they can be separated again by physical methods.
91988.m: Air is a mixture of different gases.

91989.q: Which part of the air varies most depending on the weather and place?
91989.e: Over deserts there is almost no water vapour in the air; in the tropics up to about 4 per cent. The shares of the other main gases, on the other hand, stay almost the same.
91989.m: The amount of water vapour in the air changes all the time.

91990.q: How is air separated into its parts in industry?
91990.e: In the Linde process, air is cooled strongly until it becomes liquid. Then the gases evaporate at different temperatures and can be collected separately.
91990.m: Liquid air can be split into its gases by distillation.

91991.q: What is different about the air on a high mountain such as the Matterhorn compared with the lowlands?
a: The air is thinner, but the shares stay almost the same
The air contains no more oxygen
The air consists mainly of carbon dioxide
The air contains twice as much oxygen
91991.e: Air pressure falls with height, and each breath contains fewer gas particles. But the percentage make-up of the air stays almost the same.
91991.m: High up, the air is thinner but has the same make-up.

91992.q: A ball weighs more when pumped up than when empty. What does this show?
91992.e: When pumping, extra air is pressed into the ball. Because air has mass too, the ball then weighs a little more.

91993.q: Which noble gas, at just under 1 per cent, is the third most common gas in dry air?
91993.e: Argon makes up about 0.93 per cent of the air. That makes it much more common than carbon dioxide.
91993.m: Argon is the most common noble gas in the air.

91994.q: What is the chemical symbol for argon?
91994.e: Argon has the symbol Ar. Ag stands for silver, Al for aluminium and Au for gold.
91994.m: The element symbol for argon is Ar.

91995.q: What is argon’s atomic number in the periodic table?
91995.e: An argon atom has 18 protons in its nucleus. It is in the third period on the far right with the noble gases.

91996.q: What does the Greek name argon mean?
91996.e: The Greek word “argos” means lazy or idle. The name fits because argon takes part in practically no chemical reactions.
91996.m: The name argon means “the lazy one”.

91997.q: What does argon look and smell like?
91997.e: Argon is an invisible gas with no smell. That is why you do not notice that you breathe it in with every breath.

91998.q: What is argon used for in welding?
a: As a shielding gas against oxygen in the air
91998.e: Argon surrounds the hot weld. That way the oxygen in the air cannot attack the liquid metal.
91998.m: In welding, argon protects the metal from oxygen.

91999.q: Why were classic light bulbs filled with argon instead of air?
a: So that the filament does not burn up
So that the bulb glows in colour
So that the bulb is lighter
So that the current flows better
91999.e: In air, the glowing tungsten wire would react with oxygen and burn through. Unreactive argon therefore makes the bulb last longer.
91999.m: Argon in light bulbs protects the glowing wire.

92001.q: Why is the gap in many double-glazed windows filled with argon?
a: To stop it steaming up inside
So that the glass does not get scratched
92001.e: Argon conducts heat less well than air. So less heat is lost through a window filled with argon.
92001.m: Argon in windows helps save energy.

92003.q: What is solid carbon dioxide called?
92003.e: At normal air pressure, solid carbon dioxide does not melt but turns straight into gas. Because no liquid is left behind, it is called dry ice.
92003.m: Solid carbon dioxide is called dry ice.

92004.q: What happens to dry ice when it lies at room temperature?
92004.e: Dry ice does not melt at normal air pressure. It turns straight into carbon dioxide gas, often producing white mist.
92004.m: Dry ice turns straight from a solid into a gas.

92005.q: Why is a cellar where wine is fermenting dangerous?
a: Heavy CO2 collects at the bottom
The wine catches fire by itself
92005.e: Fermentation produces a lot of carbon dioxide. It is heavier than air, collects at the bottom and pushes out the oxygen, so there is a risk of suffocation.
92005.m: Carbon dioxide is heavier than air and can be dangerous in cellars.

92006.q: Why is carbon dioxide good for putting out fires?
92006.e: A CO2 extinguisher covers the flames with a gas that does not burn. Without oxygen the fire is smothered, and no extinguishing agent is left behind.
92006.m: Carbon dioxide smothers flames because it pushes out the oxygen.

92007.q: What forms when carbon dioxide dissolves in water?
92007.e: A small part of the dissolved carbon dioxide reacts with water to form carbonic acid (H2CO3). It gives fizzy mineral water its slightly sour taste.
92007.m: Dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid with water.

92008.q: Which raising agent releases carbon dioxide during baking without the need for yeast?
92008.e: Baking powder contains bicarbonate of soda and an acid. With moisture and heat they react and form carbon dioxide, which makes the cake light.
92008.m: Baking powder lightens dough with carbon dioxide.

92009.q: Which gas makes a yeast dough rise?
92009.e: Yeast breaks down sugar in the dough and produces carbon dioxide. The gas bubbles get trapped in the dough and make it rise.
92009.m: Yeast makes dough rise with carbon dioxide.

92010.q: At what pressure can carbon dioxide be turned into a liquid?
92010.e: At normal air pressure there is no liquid carbon dioxide. It only becomes liquid from about 5.2 bar, which is how it is stored in gas cylinders and fire extinguishers.
92010.m: Liquid carbon dioxide exists only under pressure.

92011.q: What is the chemical formula of carbon monoxide?
92011.e: “Mono” means one: a molecule consists of one carbon atom and one oxygen atom.
92011.m: Carbon monoxide has the formula CO.

92012.q: When does carbon monoxide form during burning?
a: When there is too little oxygen
When the flame is especially hot
When it is put out with water
92012.e: When oxygen is short, carbon burns incompletely. Then each carbon atom gets only one oxygen atom.
92012.m: Carbon monoxide forms during incomplete burning.

92013.q: What does breathed-in carbon monoxide attach to in the body, making it so dangerous?
92013.e: Carbon monoxide takes the places meant for oxygen in the haemoglobin of red blood cells. The blood can then no longer carry enough oxygen.
92013.m: Carbon monoxide blocks oxygen transport in the blood.

92014.q: Why can’t you notice carbon monoxide in the air?
a: It is only there at night
It smells like fresh air after rain
92014.e: You cannot see, smell or taste carbon monoxide. That is why it is so treacherous, for example with faulty heaters or barbecues in closed rooms.
92014.m: Carbon monoxide is an invisible, odourless poison.

92015.q: Which device warns of dangerous carbon monoxide in homes?
92015.e: A CO alarm measures the gas with a sensor and sounds the alarm. A normal smoke alarm, by contrast, only reacts to smoke particles.
92015.m: Only a CO alarm reliably detects carbon monoxide.

92016.q: What forms when carbon monoxide burns with oxygen?
92016.e: Carbon monoxide is flammable and burns with a bluish flame. In doing so it takes up another oxygen atom.
92016.m: Carbon monoxide burns to form carbon dioxide.

92017.q: What is carbon monoxide used for in a blast furnace?
a: It removes the oxygen from the iron ore
92017.e: In the blast furnace, carbon monoxide forms from coke. It reacts with the iron oxide in the ore, producing iron and carbon dioxide.
92017.m: In the blast furnace, carbon monoxide acts as a reducing agent.

92018.q: What should you do if a CO alarm goes off?
a: Open the windows, leave the room and get help
Switch off the alarm and go back to sleep
92018.e: Carbon monoxide is an invisible poison. Fresh air and leaving the room quickly protect you from poisoning.
92018.m: If a CO alarm sounds, air the room at once and leave.

92019.q: What is the formula of nitrogen dioxide?
92019.e: A molecule of nitrogen dioxide consists of one nitrogen atom and two oxygen atoms.
92019.m: Nitrogen dioxide has the formula NO2.

92020.q: Which source gives off the most nitrogen oxides in towns and cities?
92020.e: Nitrogen oxides form mainly in engines, especially diesel engines. So levels are highest beside busy roads.
92020.m: Road traffic is the main source of nitrogen oxides.

92021.q: What colour is nitrogen dioxide gas?
92021.e: Nitrogen dioxide is a reddish-brown gas with a sharp smell. In high concentrations it turns the air over cities brownish.
92021.m: Nitrogen dioxide is a reddish-brown gas.

92022.q: Mainly from what do nitrogen oxides form during burning?
a: From nitrogen and oxygen in the air
92022.e: At very high temperatures, even the unreactive nitrogen in the air reacts with oxygen. The hotter the burning, the more nitrogen oxides form.
92022.m: Nitrogen oxides form from the gases of the air at high temperatures.

92023.q: Which part of a car turns nitrogen oxides into harmless nitrogen?
92023.e: In the catalytic converter, exhaust gases react on a layer of precious metal. Nitrogen oxides are turned into nitrogen and carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide.
92023.m: The catalytic converter makes car exhaust less harmful.

92024.q: Which acid can form from nitrogen oxides in the air and cause acid rain?
92024.e: Nitrogen oxides react with water and oxygen in the air to form nitric acid. It falls with the rain onto soils, forests and buildings.
92024.m: Nitrogen oxides contribute to acid rain through nitric acid.

92025.q: In summer, nitrogen oxides play an important part in forming which pollutant near the ground?
92025.e: In strong sunlight, nitrogen oxides react with other exhaust gases to form ozone. That is why ozone levels often rise above the limit on hot summer days.
92025.m: Nitrogen oxides and sunshine produce ground-level ozone in summer.

92026.q: What is the colourless nitrogen oxide with the formula NO called?
92026.e: Nitrogen monoxide forms directly during burning. In the air it quickly reacts further with oxygen to form nitrogen dioxide.
92026.m: Nitrogen monoxide has the formula NO.

92027.q: What does the label PM10 mean for fine dust?
a: Dust from a height of 10 metres
Dust that stays in the air for 10 days
92027.e: PM stands for “particulate matter”. PM10 covers all particles with a diameter under 10 micrometres, so finer than a hair.
92027.m: PM10 means dust particles less than ten micrometres across.

92028.q: Which type of heating contributes a lot to fine dust pollution in Switzerland in winter?
92028.e: Above all, old or badly used wood stoves release a lot of soot and fine dust. Dry wood and lighting the fire correctly can reduce this greatly.
92028.m: Badly run wood stoves produce a lot of fine dust.

92029.q: Why is very fine dust especially harmful to health?
a: It gets deep into the lungs
92029.e: The nose and the bronchial tubes filter out coarse particles. But very small particles reach the air sacs of the lungs and some even get into the blood.
92029.m: The finer the dust, the deeper it gets into the lungs.

92030.q: What do air quality stations in Switzerland measure, for example?
a: The amount of fine dust in the air
92030.e: Measuring stations constantly record how much fine dust and other pollutants are in the air. That way people know whether the air is healthy.
92030.m: Measuring stations monitor fine dust in the air.

92031.q: In which weather situation does especially high fine dust build up in the Swiss Plateau in winter?
a: During a strong bise wind and sunshine
92031.e: In an inversion, warm air lies above cold air. Then the air hardly mixes, and pollutants collect beneath the layer of fog.
92031.m: Inversions trap fine dust near the ground.

92032.q: Which device holds back the soot in the exhaust of diesel engines?
92032.e: A particulate filter catches the soot particles from the exhaust. From time to time the soot in the filter is burnt off at a high temperature.
92032.m: Particulate filters greatly reduce soot from diesel engines.

92033.q: What does a limit value for fine dust set?
a: The most fine dust allowed in the air
How much dust you may have at home
How many trees may be cut down
92033.e: Limit values protect health. If too much fine dust is measured, measures must be taken.
92033.m: A limit value says the most fine dust that is allowed.

92034.q: Where does some of the fine dust from traffic come from, which electric cars produce too?
a: From wear on tyres and brakes
92034.e: When driving and braking, tyres, brake pads and road surfaces wear away. These particles form no matter how the car is powered.
92034.m: Wear on tyres and brakes is an important source of fine dust.

92035.q: Which type of current is used for the electrolysis of water?
92035.e: Only with direct current does each pole always stay plus or always minus. So the same gas always forms at each electrode and can be collected separately.

92036.q: In what volume ratio do hydrogen and oxygen form in the electrolysis of water?
92036.e: Every water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. So twice as much hydrogen gas forms as oxygen gas.
92036.m: Electrolysis of water produces twice as much hydrogen as oxygen.

92037.q: Which energy conversion takes place in electrolysis?
92037.e: In electrolysis, an electric current forces a chemical reaction. The energy is then stored in the products of the reaction.
92037.m: Electrolysis stores electrical energy in substances.

92038.q: What is the positive pole in electrolysis called?
92038.e: The positive pole is called the anode, the negative one the cathode. At the anode, particles give up electrons.
92038.m: In electrolysis, the anode is the positive pole.

92039.q: How can you tell that a reaction is taking place in the electrolysis of water?
92039.e: Bubbles rise at both poles. Hydrogen forms at one pole and oxygen at the other.
92039.m: In the electrolysis of water, gas bubbles form at the poles.

92040.q: Why do you add a little acid or salt to the water for electrolysis?
a: Because pure water conducts electricity poorly
So that the water does not freeze
So that the gases become coloured
92040.e: Pure water contains only very few ions. Acid or salt provide extra ions that conduct the current.
92040.m: Ions in the water are what make electrolysis really work.

92041.q: Which device reverses the electrolysis of water and produces electricity from hydrogen and oxygen?
92041.e: In a fuel cell, hydrogen and oxygen react in a controlled way to form water. Electrical energy is released.
92041.m: A fuel cell produces electricity from hydrogen and oxygen.

92042.q: Which metal was produced using electrolysis at Neuhausen am Rheinfall from 1888?
92042.e: Aluminium can only be obtained with a lot of electricity by molten salt electrolysis. The water power of the Rhine Falls supplied the energy needed.
92042.m: Aluminium is obtained by electrolysis using a lot of electricity.

92043.q: What is hydrogen made by electrolysis using electricity from renewable energy called?
92043.e: If the electricity for electrolysis comes from sun, wind or water power, hardly any CO2 is produced. Hydrogen from natural gas, by contrast, is called grey.
92043.m: Green hydrogen is made with renewable electricity.

92044.q: Which dissolved particles make water hard?
92044.e: On its way through the ground, water dissolves calcium and magnesium out of the rock. The more of these is dissolved, the harder the water.
92044.m: Calcium and magnesium decide how hard water is.

92045.q: What is water called from which practically all dissolved salts have been removed, for example for a steam iron?
92045.e: In distilling, water is evaporated and the steam condensed again. The dissolved salts stay behind, so this water forms no limescale.
92045.m: Distilled water contains almost no dissolved salts.

92046.q: Which substance builds up in the kettle with hard water?
92046.e: When hard water is heated, calcium carbonate comes out of it. This white layer is called limescale or scale.
92046.m: Hard water leaves limescale in the kettle.

92047.q: How does an ion exchanger soften water?
a: It filters out sand and gravel
92047.e: In the ion exchanger, calcium and magnesium ions are held on a resin. In return, the resin releases sodium ions, which do not form limescale.
92047.m: An ion exchanger makes hard water soft.

92048.q: What is the chemical formula of limestone (calcium carbonate)?
92048.e: Calcium carbonate consists of calcium, carbon and oxygen. In nature it occurs as limestone, marble and chalk.
92048.m: Calcium carbonate has the formula CaCO3.

92049.q: What is spring water usually like if it has only flowed through granite and gneiss?
92049.e: Granite and gneiss contain hardly any lime that could dissolve. So water from such areas, for example in parts of the Alps, tends to be soft.
92049.m: Water from rock with little lime is soft.

92050.q: Why does soap lather poorly in very hard water?
a: It forms insoluble scum with calcium
92050.e: The calcium ions combine with the soap to form an insoluble coating. Some of the soap then no longer works.
92050.m: In hard water you need more soap.

92051.q: What does it mean if the tap water where you live is very hard?
a: It contains a lot of dissolved lime
It contains a lot of sugar
It is as sour as vinegar
92051.e: Hard water contains a lot of dissolved calcium and magnesium. So it quickly forms limescale in the kettle.
92051.m: Hard water contains a lot of dissolved lime.

92052.q: Roughly what is the density of ice?
92052.e: Ice weighs about 0.92 grams per cubic centimetre, which makes it lighter than liquid water. So a litre of ice weighs only about 920 grams.
92052.m: Ice is a little lighter than liquid water.

92053.q: Why does ice float on water?
a: Ice has a lower density than water
Ice contains air bubbles of nitrogen
Ice is lighter because it is cold
Ice is carried by the wind
92053.e: When water freezes, its molecules arrange themselves in a loose lattice. So ice takes up more space and is lighter than the same amount of liquid water.
92053.m: Ice floats because it is less dense than water.

92054.q: Why can fish survive the winter in a frozen lake?
a: The lake freezes from the top down
The water only freezes at night
92054.e: The coldest water stays at the top and freezes first. The layer of ice insulates, and liquid water remains at the bottom.
92054.m: Lakes freeze from the top, so fish survive the winter.

92055.q: By roughly how much does the volume of water increase when it freezes?
92055.e: 100 litres of water become about 109 litres of ice. This expansion is very unusual for a liquid.
92055.m: Freezing water expands by about a tenth.

92056.q: What is the process called in which freezing water breaks up rocks in the Alps?
92056.e: Water gets into cracks in the rock. When it freezes, it expands and pushes the cracks apart until pieces break off.
92056.m: In frost shattering, freezing water breaks up rock.

92057.q: Why can a full, closed glass bottle of water burst in the freezer?
a: Overpressure builds up in the freezer
92057.e: Ice needs more space than liquid water. In a full bottle it has no room and bursts the glass.
92057.m: Full water bottles burst when they freeze.

92059.q: Roughly what part of an iceberg lies below the surface of the water?
92059.e: Ice is only a little lighter than sea water. So only about a tenth of an iceberg sticks out of the water.
92059.m: You only see the tip of an iceberg.

92060.q: Where does about 80 per cent of Swiss drinking water come from?
92060.e: About 40 per cent of drinking water comes from springs and about 40 per cent from groundwater. The remaining 20 per cent or so is taken from lakes.
92060.m: Most Swiss drinking water comes from underground.

92061.q: How can germs in drinking water be killed without adding any chemicals?
92061.e: Ultraviolet light damages the genetic material of bacteria and viruses so that they can no longer multiply. Many Swiss water suppliers use this method.
92061.m: UV light disinfects water without chemicals.

92062.q: What job does a sand filter do in a waterworks?
92062.e: The water trickles slowly through layers of sand and gravel. Cloudy matter and fine particles get caught.
92062.m: Sand filters make cloudy water clear.

92063.q: What is activated carbon used for in treating drinking water?
a: To bind smells and trace substances
92063.e: Activated carbon has a huge inner surface with many pores. Substances that spoil the taste and smell, as well as many residues, stick to it.
92063.m: Activated carbon binds unwanted substances on its large surface.

92064.q: Which substance is sometimes added to the water mains so that the water stays free of germs all the way to the tap?
92064.e: A small amount of chlorine or chlorine dioxide keeps working against germs in the pipes. But in many Swiss municipalities the water is so clean that this is not needed.
92064.m: Chlorine can keep drinking water germ-free in the pipes.

92065.q: Which gas with three oxygen atoms is used for disinfection in lake waterworks?
92065.e: Ozone (O3) is a very strong oxidising agent. It kills germs and breaks down many smelly substances and pollutants.
92065.m: Ozone is used to disinfect lake water.

92066.q: What does a flocculant do in water treatment?
92066.e: The flocculant makes tiny floating particles clump into larger flakes. These can then easily settle or be filtered out.
92066.m: Flocculants make small dirt particles filterable.

92067.q: From which body of water does the city of Zurich get most of its drinking water?
92067.e: About 70 per cent of Zurich’s drinking water comes from Lake Zurich. It is treated in several stages at the Lengg and Moos lake waterworks.
92067.m: Zurich mainly drinks treated lake water.

92068.q: What is the most important solvent on Earth?
92068.e: Water dissolves very many substances, such as salts, sugar and gases. In our bodies and in nature, almost all chemical processes take place in water.
92068.m: Water is the most important solvent.

92069.q: Which of these substances dissolves well in water?
92069.e: Salts are made of ions that get surrounded by water molecules. Fats and waxes, on the other hand, do not dissolve in water.
92069.m: Table salt dissolves well in water, but fat does not.

92070.q: Which solvent is found in many nail varnish removers?
92070.e: Acetone quickly dissolves the plastics in nail varnish. It evaporates fast and catches fire easily.
92070.m: Acetone is a well-known solvent for nail varnish.

92071.q: What do you call a solution in which no more of a substance will dissolve at the same temperature?
92071.e: In a saturated solution, the largest possible amount of a substance is dissolved. If you add more, it stays at the bottom as sediment.
92071.m: Nothing more dissolves in a saturated solution.

92072.q: Why does warm fizzy mineral water lose its fizz faster than cold?
a: Gases dissolve less well when warm
The bottle seals better when warm
92072.e: Unlike sugar or salt, gases become less soluble as the temperature rises. So the dissolved carbon dioxide escapes faster.
92072.m: Gases dissolve better in cold water than in warm.

92073.q: Why is water so good at dissolving salts?
92073.e: A water molecule has a slightly negative end and a slightly positive end. This lets it surround positive and negative ions and pull them out of the salt crystal.
92073.m: Polar water molecules pull ions out of salt crystals.

92074.q: How does sugar dissolve faster in tea?
a: By stirring it in hot tea
By leaving it still in cold tea
With an ice cube in the tea
With a lid on the cup
92074.e: Heat and stirring get the particles moving. That way the sugar dissolves much faster.
92074.m: Heat and stirring speed up dissolving.

92075.q: What removes a grease stain better than plain water?
a: A non-polar solvent such as white spirit
92075.e: Following the rule “like dissolves like”, non-polar fats dissolve in non-polar solvents. Water, by contrast, is polar.
92075.m: Fat dissolves in non-polar solvents, not in water.

92076.q: You dissolve 20 g of salt in 180 g of water. What is the mass fraction of the salt?
92076.e: The solution weighs 20 g + 180 g = 200 g. The mass fraction is 20 g ÷ 200 g = 0.10, so 10 %.
92076.m: For the mass fraction, you divide by the mass of the whole solution.

92077.q: How much sugar do 500 g of a sugar solution with a mass fraction of 5 % contain?
92077.e: You work out 5 % of 500 g as 500 g times 0.05. That gives 25 g of sugar.
92077.m: The mass of the dissolved substance is the mass fraction times the mass of the solution.

92078.q: You dissolve 50 g of sugar in 200 g of water. What is the mass fraction of the sugar?
92078.e: The solution weighs 50 g + 200 g = 250 g. The mass fraction is 50 g ÷ 250 g = 0.20, so 20 %.
92078.m: The solvent also counts towards the total mass of the solution.

92079.q: How do you calculate the mass fraction of a substance in a mixture?
a: Mass of the substance divided by mass of the mixture
Mass of the mixture divided by mass of the substance
Mass of the substance times volume of the mixture
Volume of the substance divided by its mass
92079.e: The mass fraction tells you what share of the total mass belongs to one substance. You divide the mass of the substance by the mass of the whole mixture.
92079.m: The mass fraction is a ratio of two masses.

92080.q: Sea water has a salt mass fraction of about 3.5 %. How much salt do 2 kg of sea water contain?
92080.e: 2 kg is 2000 g. 2000 g times 0.035 gives 70 g of salt.
92080.m: Sea water contains about 35 grams of salt per kilogram.

92081.q: You add 200 g of water to 300 g of a 10 per cent salt solution. What is the new mass fraction?
92081.e: The solution contains 300 g times 0.10 = 30 g of salt. After diluting it weighs 500 g, so the share is 30 g ÷ 500 g = 6 %.
92081.m: When diluting, the mass of the dissolved substance stays the same.

92082.q: You dissolve 12 g of salt in 228 g of water. What is the mass fraction of the salt?
92082.e: The solution weighs 12 g + 228 g = 240 g. The mass fraction is 12 g ÷ 240 g = 0.05, so 5 %.
92082.m: First work out the mass of the whole solution.

92083.q: How much water do you need to make 400 g of a salt solution with a mass fraction of 15 %?
92083.e: The solution contains 400 g times 0.15 = 60 g of salt. The rest is water: 400 g minus 60 g = 340 g.
92083.m: The mass of the solvent is the total mass minus the mass of the dissolved substance.

92084.q: Roughly what is the mass fraction of oxygen in water (H2O), if H has a mass of 1 u and O a mass of 16 u?
92084.e: A water molecule has a mass of 2 times 1 u + 16 u = 18 u. The oxygen share is 16 ÷ 18, about 0.89, so around 89 %.
92084.m: By mass, water is mostly oxygen.

92184.e: Blaise Pascal started building this machine in 1642. It could add numbers and was named after him.
92184.m: The Pascaline was invented by Blaise Pascal.

92185.q: Who did Blaise Pascal originally build his calculating machine for?
a: For his father, a tax official
92185.e: As a tax official, Pascal's father had to add up a great many numbers. The machine was meant to make this work easier for him.
92185.m: Pascal built the Pascaline to help his father with calculations.

92186.q: In which century did Blaise Pascal build his calculating machine?
92186.e: Pascal presented his calculating machine in 1645. That was in the 17th century, long before there was electricity in everyday life.
92186.m: The Pascaline was made in the 17th century.

92187.q: Which kind of calculation could the Pascaline carry out directly?
92187.e: The Pascaline was mainly an adding machine. Subtraction was only possible in a roundabout way using complement numbers.
92187.m: The Pascaline could mainly add numbers.

92188.q: How did you set the numbers on the Pascaline?
92188.e: There was a dial for each place. The result appeared in small windows above the dials.
92188.m: On the Pascaline you turned dials to enter numbers.

92189.q: Was the Pascaline an electric or a mechanical machine?
92189.e: In the 17th century there was no electricity in everyday life yet. The Pascaline worked purely mechanically with wheels and levers.
92189.m: The Pascaline was a purely mechanical calculating machine.

92190.q: Pascal built about 50 test models of his calculating machine. What does this show?
a: It took a lot of trying out before it worked well
He got the machine right at the first attempt
He wanted to give away 50 machines
92190.e: Pascal improved his machine again and again until it calculated reliably. Inventing often means trying things out, finding mistakes and improving.
92190.m: Pascal built about 50 test models of his calculating machine.

92191.q: When adding, what did a calculating machine like the Pascaline have to pass on automatically when a place went over 9?
92191.e: When a wheel jumps from 9 to 0, the next wheel has to be turned on by one. This is called carrying.
92191.m: When carrying, a one is passed on to the next place.

92192.q: How is information stored on a punched card?
92192.e: Whether there is a hole in a place or not carries the information. A machine senses the holes.
92192.m: A punched card stores data with holes.

92193.q: For which machine were punched cards already used around 1805 to control patterns?
92193.e: Joseph-Marie Jacquard used punched cards to control which threads were lifted during weaving. This created complicated fabric patterns automatically.
92193.m: Even looms were controlled with punched cards.

92194.q: What did Herman Hollerith use punched cards for in the USA in 1890?
92194.e: Hollerith developed machines that counted punched cards with details of each person. This meant the 1890 census could be analysed much faster.
92194.m: Hollerith counted the 1890 US census with punched cards.

92195.q: Which well-known computer company grew out of Herman Hollerith's firm?
92195.e: In 1911 Hollerith's firm became part of a merger which from 1924 was called International Business Machines (IBM).
92195.m: IBM grew out of Herman Hollerith's firm.

92196.q: What did you have to do if you had punched a wrong hole in a punched card?
92196.e: A punched hole cannot be closed again. That is why you punched the whole card again.
92196.m: Mistakes on punched cards could not be deleted.

92197.q: What happened if a programmer dropped a stack of punched cards?
a: The order of the program lines got mixed up
92197.e: Often one line of a program was on one card. So the order was important, and many programmers numbered their cards.
92197.m: With punched cards the correct order was very important.

92198.q: What was the device called that punched holes in punched cards?
92198.e: With a card punch you typed in characters, and the device punched the matching holes in the card.
92198.m: With a card punch you punched the holes in the card.

92199.q: What was one advantage of punched cards over handwritten lists?
a: Machines could read and sort them automatically
You could read them under water
92199.e: Punched cards could be counted, sorted and analysed by machines. This saved a lot of manual work.
92199.m: Punched cards could be read by machines.

92200.q: Which country did Charles Babbage come from?
92200.e: Charles Babbage was born in London in 1791. He was a mathematician, inventor and professor at Cambridge.
92200.m: Charles Babbage was an English mathematician.

92201.q: Which nickname is Charles Babbage often given?
92201.e: In the 19th century, Babbage designed calculating machines that already anticipated important parts of today's computer.
92201.m: Charles Babbage is considered the father of the computer.

92202.q: What was the name of Babbage's machine that was meant to calculate mathematical tables without errors?
92202.e: The Difference Engine was meant to calculate tables of numbers automatically. At that time, tables calculated by hand often contained errors.
92202.m: Babbage's Difference Engine was meant to calculate tables without errors.

92203.q: What was the name of Babbage's design for a freely programmable calculating machine?
92203.e: The Analytical Engine already had a calculating unit and a memory. It is considered a forerunner of the computer.
92203.m: The Analytical Engine was Babbage's design for a computer.

92204.q: Was the Analytical Engine completed during Babbage's lifetime?
a: Yes, there was one in every school
92204.e: The machine was too complicated and too expensive for the technology of the time. Babbage died in 1871 without completing it.
92204.m: Babbage's Analytical Engine was never completed.

92205.q: Which museum built a working Difference Engine from Babbage's plans in 1991?
a: The Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne
92205.e: The Science Museum in London built Difference Engine No. 2 from Babbage's drawings. It worked and proved that his plans were correct.
92205.m: Babbage's Difference Engine works, as a reconstruction from 1991 shows.

92206.q: How were Babbage's calculating machines meant to be powered?
a: Mechanically, with gears and a crank or steam power
92206.e: Babbage's machines consisted of thousands of gears and shafts. Electricity was not yet available as a power source.
92206.m: Babbage's machines were mechanical and had many gears.

92207.q: Into which two main parts did Babbage divide his Analytical Engine?
92207.e: Babbage called the calculating unit the “Mill” and the memory the “Store”. This division can still be found in today's computers.
92207.m: Babbage divided his machine into a calculating unit and a memory.

92208.q: Which title is Ada Lovelace often given in the history of computing?
92208.e: In her notes she described an exact sequence of steps for how a machine should carry out a calculation. This is considered the first computer program.
92208.m: Ada Lovelace is considered the first programmer.

92209.q: For which machine did Ada Lovelace write her famous program in 1843?
a: For a calculating machine by Charles Babbage
92209.e: Ada Lovelace wrote a step-by-step plan for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine. The program was meant to calculate the Bernoulli numbers.
92209.m: Ada Lovelace wrote a program for the Bernoulli numbers.

92210.q: Which programming language was named in honour of Ada Lovelace?
92210.e: The programming language Ada was developed around 1980 for the US Department of Defense and named after her.
92210.m: The programming language Ada bears the name of Ada Lovelace.

92211.q: What did Ada Lovelace foresee for calculating machines?
a: That they could not only calculate but also, for example, process music
92211.e: She realised that a machine like this could work with all kinds of symbols, such as musical notes. That was a very modern idea.
92211.m: Ada Lovelace realised that machines can process more than just numbers.

92212.q: Who is honoured on the yearly Ada Lovelace Day?
92212.e: Ada Lovelace Day takes place on the second Tuesday in October. It celebrates women in science and technology.
92212.m: On Ada Lovelace Day women in technology and science are honoured.

92213.q: Which computer did Konrad Zuse complete in Berlin in 1941?
92213.e: The Z3 is considered the world's first working, program-controlled and fully automatic digital computer.
92213.m: Konrad Zuse built the Z3 in 1941.

92214.q: Which number system did Konrad Zuse's computers calculate with?
92214.e: Zuse used the binary system with only two digits, 0 and 1. This suits switches that are on or off.
92214.m: Zuse calculated with the binary system of zeros and ones.

92215.q: Which electrical components did the Z3 mainly consist of?
92215.e: The Z3 contained about 2000 relays. These are electromagnetic switches that clicked audibly while calculating.
92215.m: The Z3 calculated with clicking relays.

92216.q: What was Konrad Zuse's Z1 from 1938?
92216.e: The Z1 consisted of thousands of sheet metal parts and worked mechanically. It was often unreliable, because the parts got jammed.
92216.m: Zuse's first computer, the Z1, was mechanical.

92217.q: What happened to Zuse's Z3 in 1943?
a: It was destroyed in a bombing raid
It was put on display in a museum
It was mounted on a rocket
92217.e: During the Second World War the Z3 was destroyed in an air raid on Berlin. Today there are reconstructions.
92217.m: The original Z3 was destroyed in the Second World War.

92218.q: What did Konrad Zuse design in the 1940s besides his computers?
92218.e: Zuse designed Plankalkül, a language for programming computers. It is considered the first high-level programming language.
92218.m: Konrad Zuse also designed a programming language.

92219.q: Which university rented Zuse's Z4 computer in 1950?
92219.e: ETH Zurich rented the Z4 from 1950 to 1955. This meant one of the first computers in Europe was in Switzerland.
92219.m: Zuse's Z4 was at ETH Zurich from 1950 to 1955.

92220.q: In which country was the ENIAC built?
92220.e: The ENIAC was built at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia and presented to the public in 1946.
92220.m: The ENIAC was built in the USA.

92221.q: In which year was the ENIAC presented to the public?
92221.e: The ENIAC was shown to the public on 14 February 1946. It was built from 1943 onwards.

92222.q: Which components did the ENIAC calculate with?
92222.e: The ENIAC contained about 17,500 valves. That is why it was much faster than computers with mechanical parts.

92223.q: Roughly how heavy was the ENIAC?
92223.e: The ENIAC weighed about 27 tonnes and filled a whole large room.
92223.m: The ENIAC was as heavy as several lorries.

92224.q: What was the ENIAC originally meant to do calculations for?
a: For flight path tables for the US Army
92224.e: The US Army needed tables showing how shells fly. These ballistic calculations took a very long time by hand.
92224.m: The ENIAC first did calculations for the US Army.

92225.q: How was the ENIAC programmed at first?
a: By replugging cables and setting switches
92225.e: For every new task, cables had to be reconnected and rotary switches set. This could take days.
92225.m: The ENIAC was programmed with cables and switches.

92226.e: The first programmers of the ENIAC were women such as Jean Bartik and Betty Holberton. Today they are called the “ENIAC women”.
92226.m: The ENIAC was mainly programmed by women.

92227.q: What does the abbreviation ENIAC stand for?
a: European Network for Internet And Computing
92227.e: ENIAC means Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer.
92227.m: ENIAC is the abbreviation for an electronic computer.

92228.q: What does the name ERMETH stand for?
a: First calculating machine with electrical engineering
92228.e: ERMETH is short for the German “Elektronische Rechenmaschine der ETH”, the electronic calculating machine of ETH. It was developed in Zurich.
92228.m: The ERMETH was the calculating machine of ETH Zurich.

92229.q: What is special about the ERMETH for Switzerland?
a: It was the first computer built in Switzerland
It was the first pocket calculator
It was the first games console
92229.e: The ERMETH was developed and built at ETH Zurich itself. It is considered the first computer from Switzerland.
92229.m: The ERMETH was the first computer built in Switzerland.

92230.q: In which city was the ERMETH built?
92230.e: The ERMETH was created in the 1950s at ETH Zurich under the direction of the mathematician Eduard Stiefel.
92230.m: The ERMETH was built at ETH in Zurich.

92231.q: What served as the ERMETH's working memory?
92231.e: The memory was a magnetic drum weighing about 1.5 tonnes. It turned 100 times per second.
92231.m: The ERMETH stored data on a magnetic drum.

92232.q: Roughly how many valves did the ERMETH's calculating unit contain?
92232.e: The ERMETH's calculating unit consisted of about 1500 valves.
92232.m: The ERMETH calculated with about 1500 valves.

92233.q: Where can you see the ERMETH today?
a: In the Museum of Communication in Bern
In the Swiss National Museum in Zurich
In the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne
In the Federal Palace in Bern
92233.e: Since 2006 the ERMETH has been on permanent loan from ETH to the Museum of Communication in Bern. Before that it was in the Technorama in Winterthur.
92233.m: Today the ERMETH is in the Museum of Communication in Bern.

92234.q: Why was the ERMETH replaced after a few years?
a: Newer computers were faster and smaller
It was made of wood and rotted
Nobody wanted to calculate any more
92234.e: Computer technology developed at great speed. In 1963 a more modern computer replaced the ERMETH at ETH.
92234.m: Old computers are replaced by faster and smaller ones.

92235.q: Which number system did the ERMETH calculate with?
92235.e: The ERMETH worked with decimal numbers. One memory word had 16 decimal places.
92235.m: The ERMETH calculated with decimal numbers.

92236.q: Which country did the well-known computer scientist Niklaus Wirth come from?
92236.e: Niklaus Wirth was born in Winterthur in 1934. Later he taught for many years at ETH Zurich.
92236.m: Niklaus Wirth was a Swiss computer scientist.

92237.q: At which university was Niklaus Wirth a professor of computer science from 1968 to 1999?
92237.e: Wirth taught for over 30 years at ETH Zurich and shaped computer science education there.
92237.m: Niklaus Wirth was a professor of computer science at ETH Zurich.

92238.q: Which important computer science award did Niklaus Wirth receive in 1984?
a: A gold medal at the Olympic Games
92238.e: The Turing Award is considered the “Nobel Prize of computing”. Wirth was the first German-speaking computer scientist to receive it.
92238.m: Niklaus Wirth received the Turing Award in 1984.

92239.q: What is the Swiss Niklaus Wirth famous for?
92239.e: At ETH Zurich, Niklaus Wirth developed programming languages such as Pascal and Oberon. Many people around the world learnt to program with Pascal.
92239.m: Niklaus Wirth developed programming languages such as Pascal.

92240.q: What did the computer that Niklaus Wirth's team built at ETH around 1980 already have back then?
a: A graphical screen and a mouse
92240.e: The computer was called Lilith. A screen with graphics and a mouse were new and rare at that time.
92240.m: Wirth's computer Lilith already had a mouse around 1980.

92241.q: Niklaus Wirth criticised the fact that programs keep getting bigger and more sluggish. What do you therefore often notice with new computers?
a: They still do not feel much faster
They no longer need any electricity
They can no longer open programs
92241.e: The hardware keeps getting faster, but the programs keep getting bigger too. That is why new computers often hardly feel faster.
92241.m: Big, sluggish programs slow down even fast computers.

92242.q: Which country did the famous computer scientist Niklaus Wirth come from?
92242.e: Niklaus Wirth was born in Winterthur and taught at ETH Zurich. He is one of the best-known computer scientists in the world.
92242.m: Niklaus Wirth was a Swiss computer scientist.

92243.q: What is Niklaus Wirth mainly known for?
a: He invented programming languages such as Pascal
92243.e: At ETH Zurich, Niklaus Wirth developed several programming languages. The best known is Pascal.
92243.m: Niklaus Wirth invented the programming language Pascal.

92244.q: Who developed the programming language Pascal?
92244.e: Niklaus Wirth developed Pascal at ETH Zurich. Before that he had already worked on the language Algol W.
92244.m: The language Pascal comes from Niklaus Wirth.

92245.q: Who was the programming language Pascal named after?
92245.e: The language honours the French mathematician and philosopher Blaise Pascal, who lived in the 17th century.
92245.m: Pascal is named after Blaise Pascal.

92247.q: What was Pascal especially popular for?
92247.e: Pascal was deliberately built in a clear way. That is why the language was used for teaching at schools and universities around the world.
92247.m: Pascal was a popular language for teaching programming.

a: An operating system for mobile phones
92248.e: Pascal is a programming language. With it you write commands that a computer can carry out.

92249.q: Which words begin and end a block of instructions in Pascal?
92249.e: In Pascal you group several instructions together between begin and end. The main program ends with end and a full stop.
92249.m: In Pascal, blocks go between begin and end.

92250.q: What did you need a program like Turbo Pascal for?
a: To write and run programs in Pascal
92250.e: Turbo Pascal was a development environment. In it you could write, compile and run Pascal programs.
92250.m: Many people programmed on the PC with Turbo Pascal.

92251.q: Which command in Pascal outputs text on the screen and moves to the next line?
92251.e: The command writeln stands for “write line”. For example, writeln('Hello') outputs the word Hello.
92251.m: In Pascal you output text with writeln.

92252.q: Which organisation did Grace Hopper work for for a long time, finally becoming an admiral?
92252.e: Grace Hopper joined the US Navy during the Second World War. She rose to the rank of rear admiral.
92252.m: Grace Hopper was a computer scientist and an admiral in the US Navy.

92253.q: What did Grace Hopper develop in 1952 as one of the first programs of its kind?
92253.e: A compiler automatically translates program text into machine language. Hopper's A-0 is considered one of the first compilers.
92253.m: Grace Hopper developed one of the first compilers.

92254.q: What did Grace Hopper want to achieve with her programming languages?
a: That programs could be written with words that are almost English
That computers would run without electricity
That only soldiers would be allowed to program
That programs would consist only of numbers
92254.e: Hopper thought programs should be readable for people. That is why the language COBOL, which she shaped, uses many English words.
92254.m: Grace Hopper wanted to make programs as readable as English.

92256.q: What did Grace Hopper like to show with a piece of wire about 30 centimetres long?
a: How far light travels in a nanosecond
How long a computer cable has to be
How thick a punched card is
92256.e: Light travels about 30 centimetres in a billionth of a second. This was her way of showing why short wires make computers faster.
92256.m: In a nanosecond light only travels about 30 centimetres.

92257.e: Because of her achievements and her manner she was often called “Amazing Grace”, after a well-known song.

92258.q: How big was the Harvard Mark I, which Grace Hopper worked on from 1944?
a: So big that it filled a whole room
As small as a mobile phone
As big as a school exercise book
92258.e: The Harvard Mark I was a huge electromechanical computer, about 15 metres long. Hopper was one of its first programmers.
92258.m: The first large computers filled whole rooms.

92259.q: In which century was Grace Hopper born?
92259.e: Grace Hopper was born in New York in 1906 and died in 1992. 1906 belongs to the 20th century.

92260.q: Which country does the company Logitech come from?
92260.e: Logitech was founded in 1981 in the canton of Vaud. Today the company sells its products all over the world.
92260.m: Logitech is a company from Switzerland.

92261.q: In which Swiss canton was Logitech founded?
92261.e: Logitech was founded on a farm in Apples in the canton of Vaud. Its registered head office is still in Vaud today.
92261.m: Logitech comes from the canton of Vaud.

92262.q: Which products is Logitech especially known for?
92262.e: Logitech mainly makes accessories for computers, especially mice and keyboards, as well as webcams and headsets.
92262.m: Logitech is known for mice and keyboards.

92263.q: Which device for video calls does Logitech make, among other things?
92263.e: A webcam is a small camera for the computer. Logitech is one of the best-known makers of such cameras.

92264.q: How did an early computer mouse detect how you moved it?
a: With a ball underneath that turned with it
92264.e: Early mice such as the first Logitech mouse from 1982 had a ball underneath. Today mice measure movement with light.
92264.m: Early computer mice had a ball.

92265.q: What does a wireless mouse need in order to work?
a: A battery or a rechargeable battery
92265.e: Without a cable the mouse gets no power from the computer. That is why it has a battery or rechargeable battery built in.
92265.m: Wireless mice need a battery or a rechargeable battery.

92266.q: Which product did Logitech bring onto the market in 1991?
92266.e: In 1991 Logitech brought out one of the first wireless radio mice, the Cordless MouseMan.
